title: Structured Concurrency, CoroutineContext & Job
scopeHtml: Scope: structured-concurrency guarantees, CoroutineContext mechanics, Job lifecycle and parent-child links, SupervisorJob, custom scopes and who owns them, cancel vs cancelChildren, CoroutineName. Versions referenced: kotlinx.coroutines 1.8–1.10, Kotlin 2.x.

notes.title: What structured concurrency guarantees
notes.html:
The idea, simply. Imagine every task you start is a child holding its parent's hand. A child cannot wander off alone: the parent will not leave until all children are home, and if the parent has to leave in a hurry, it calls all the children back. That is structured concurrency: the lifetime of a coroutine is tied to a scope, like a variable is tied to a block { }.

The three guarantees in kotlinx.coroutines.

  1. A parent never completes before its children. coroutineScope { launch{..}; launch{..} } returns only after both are done.
  2. Cancellation flows down. Cancel the parent and every child (and grandchild) is cancelled.
  3. Failure flows up. If a child fails with a non-cancellation exception, it cancels its parent (and so siblings), unless the parent is a supervisor. The exception is not lost: it is reported at the top of the tree.

So there are no "forgotten" coroutines: you can always find who owns the work, stop it, and see its errors.

suspend fun loadScreen(): Screen = coroutineScope {
    val user = async { api.user() }
    val feed = async { api.feed() }
    Screen(user.await(), feed.await())   // if feed throws, user is cancelled too
}

What it replaces. Threads/ExecutorService/RxJava subscribe() without a CompositeDisposable: fire-and-forget. With them, "who stops this when the screen closes?" is a manual job. GlobalScope.launch is the escape hatch that breaks the guarantee (the coroutine belongs to the whole process).

Industry examples. viewModelScope in every Jetpack ViewModel (work stops in onCleared), lifecycleScope in Activities and Fragments, Ktor server request handling (one coroutine tree per request, cancelled when the client disconnects), WorkManager's CoroutineWorker (the doWork coroutine is cancelled when the work is stopped).

Real-life picture. A group school trip: the teacher (parent) cannot go home until every student is back on the bus, and if there is an emergency the teacher calls everyone back at once.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "structured concurrency means coroutines are lightweight threads". Wrong topic: it is about lifetimes.
  • Forgetting the third guarantee: failures propagate upward and cancel siblings.
  • Claiming launch inside suspend fun is automatically structured: only if it is inside coroutineScope { } or an owned scope.

notes.title: CoroutineContext as a keyed map
notes.html:
The idea, simply. A CoroutineContext is a small bag of settings that travels with a coroutine. Each setting has a label (a Key) and the bag can hold at most one setting per label. It behaves like an immutable Map<Key, Element> plus operator +.

Typical elements.

Element Key What it does
Job Job the coroutine's handle: state, parent/child links
CoroutineDispatcher ContinuationInterceptor which thread(s) run it
CoroutineName CoroutineName debug label
CoroutineExceptionHandler same last-resort handler for uncaught exceptions

Reading it. Inside any suspend code: coroutineContext[Job], coroutineContext[CoroutineName]?.name, coroutineContext[ContinuationInterceptor]. coroutineContext there is the property from the kotlin.coroutines package (the current coroutine's context), available in any suspend function. Indexing with the Key companion returns the element or null.

suspend fun whoAmI() {
    val job = coroutineContext[Job]
    val dispatcher = coroutineContext[ContinuationInterceptor] as? CoroutineDispatcher
    Log.d("T", "job=$job dispatcher=$dispatcher name=${coroutineContext[CoroutineName]}")
}

Dispatchers.Main is also an element: it is stored under ContinuationInterceptor, which is why a context can have only one dispatcher.

Industry examples. Hilt modules that provide @IoDispatcher CoroutineDispatcher and tests that swap in StandardTestDispatcher; OkHttp/Retrofit suspend calls honouring the caller's Job via the context; Crashlytics breadcrumbs from CoroutineName.

Real-life picture. A hospital wristband with slots: one slot for "ward", one for "doctor", one for "allergy". You cannot have two "ward" stickers; a new one replaces the old.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the context is a List. It is a keyed set with one element per key.
  • Thinking Dispatchers.IO has its own key; it shares ContinuationInterceptor.
  • Using coroutineContext and not knowing it comes from a different place inside a CoroutineScope receiver (see the scope section).

notes.title: Context plus, minusKey and writing a Key
notes.html:
The rule. a + b returns a new context with everything from a, then everything from b. On a key collision, the right-hand side wins. Nothing is mutated.

val ctx = Dispatchers.Main + CoroutineName("ui") + Dispatchers.IO
// result: IO dispatcher, name "ui"  (IO replaced Main)
val noName = ctx.minusKey(CoroutineName)   // removes the element for that key

Internally a combined context is a CombinedContext(left, element) linked list. fold walks it, and get(key) searches from the element backwards. For fast dispatching the ContinuationInterceptor is kept toward the end of the chain so it is found quickly (an implementation detail; do not rely on it).

Defining a Key. Use the companion object as the Key; extend AbstractCoroutineContextElement:

class RequestId(val id: String) : AbstractCoroutineContextElement(RequestId) {
    companion object Key : CoroutineContext.Key<RequestId>
    override fun toString() = "RequestId($id)"
}

Override-order bug. scope.launch(Dispatchers.Main + Dispatchers.IO) runs on IO. A helper that appends Dispatchers.Main last after a caller passed IO silently moves the work to the UI thread: "why is my DB call on the main thread (StrictMode violation)?" Always check which side ends up on the right.

Real-life picture. Stacking transparent sheets with stamps: if two sheets have a stamp in the same box, the top sheet's stamp covers the lower one.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing + is commutative. It is not: order decides who wins.
  • Thinking minusKey mutates the context.
  • Passing the element instance rather than the Key object to minusKey or get.

notes.title: CoroutineName and debugging
notes.html:
The idea. CoroutineName("sync-contacts") is a free label. Add it where a coroutine is born; it is inherited by children.

How to see it at runtime.

  • Thread name (JVM debug mode). When coroutine debug mode is on (-Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug, and by default on JVM with assertions on), the executing thread's name becomes DefaultDispatcher-worker-1 @sync-contacts#42. This is a debugging feature and is generally not on in an Android release build; confirm in the docs for your version.
  • Logging. Log.d("T", "${coroutineContext[CoroutineName]}").
  • Android Studio's Coroutine Debugger and DebugProbes (JVM) list coroutines with names and creation stack traces.
  • Crash reports. If an exception goes uncaught, the default message includes the coroutine context (e.g. StandaloneCoroutine{Cancelling}@abc and with names, [CoroutineName(sync), ...]) in the suppressed "coroutine context" information. Crashlytics logs therefore become readable if you named your coroutines.
  • Perfetto/systrace. You can use Trace.beginSection(name) in a wrapper element, since the name itself does not become a trace slice automatically.
scope.launch(CoroutineName("upload-batch")) { upload() }

Industry examples. Teams naming viewModelScope.launch(CoroutineName("FeedVM.refresh")) so ANR traces and Crashlytics clearly show which call crashed; Ktor names its request coroutines.

Real-life picture. Names on lunchboxes in the school fridge: you can tell whose is whose.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting the name to appear in Logcat thread names automatically in release.
  • Thinking CoroutineName changes behaviour. It never does.
  • Forgetting that a child launch(CoroutineName("x")) replaces the parent's name for that child only.

notes.title: Context inheritance for launch
notes.html:
The exact formula. When you call scope.launch(ctx) { }:

newContext = scope.coroutineContext + ctx          (right side wins)
           + (the coroutine's own NEW Job)         (always fresh)
parent of the new Job = the Job found in (scope.coroutineContext + ctx)
  • Inherited: dispatcher, name, exception handler, and any custom element from the scope, unless ctx overrides them.
  • Never inherited: the Job. Every coroutine makes its own Job, whose parent is whatever Job sits in the resulting context.
  • Dispatchers.Default is used if neither the scope nor ctx supplies a dispatcher.

For a suspend call inside a coroutine, withContext(ctx) uses the current coroutine context plus ctx.

The launch(Job()) bug. If you pass a Job in ctx, it replaces the scope's Job in the computed context, so the new coroutine becomes a child of that Job, not of the scope:

viewModelScope.launch(SupervisorJob()) { loadAll() }   // BUG

Result: viewModelScope is cancelled in onCleared, but this coroutine's parent is a standalone SupervisorJob() nobody cancels. The work keeps running, holds lambdas and the ViewModel (hence LeakCanary "ViewModel retained after leaving screen"), and also the parent does not wait for it. In the stale-search scenario this also breaks "cancel previous query": jobs started under different anonymous parents are not cancelled together. Nothing even needs the Supervisor: launch's children are already independent of siblings if the scope is a supervisor.

Fix. Never pass Job()/SupervisorJob() to launch/async. To change failure policy for a block use supervisorScope { }; to run independent children, make the scope's own Job a SupervisorJob.

Real-life picture. A new hire told "your manager is now Bob from another company": they still sit in your office but the company can no longer send them home at closing time.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "the child inherits the parent's Job". It gets a new Job whose parent is the context's Job.
  • Believing launch(SupervisorJob()) makes just that coroutine a supervisor. It detaches it from structured concurrency.
  • Search "stale result" bug: not keeping the previous Job to cancel (searchJob?.cancel()), or using collectLatest/flatMapLatest instead.

notes.title: Job lifecycle states
notes.html:
The idea. A Job is a small state machine. "My code finished" is not the same as "my job is complete": a parent waits for its children.

State isActive isCompleted isCancelled
New (LAZY, not started) false false false
Active (running) true false false
Completing (body done, waiting for children) true false false
Cancelling (cancelled/failed, waiting for children to finish) false false true
Cancelled (final) false true true
Completed (final, success) false true false

Key facts:

  • isCompleted becomes true for both terminal states (cancelled counts as completed).
  • isActive is true in "Completing"; so a coroutine whose body finished may still be active.
  • join() waits for the terminal state; await() on Deferred waits for the result.
  • start() moves New to Active; join() also starts it (for LAZY).
  • job.cancel() on a Cancelling job is a no-op.
val parent = scope.launch {
    launch { delay(5_000) }   // child
    println("body done")     // parent is now Completing
}
// parent.isActive == true here, isCompleted == false until child ends

Join bugs. A common production bug is "join returns instantly" for an already-cancelled job and then the code reads state that the cancelled job never wrote. Another: you cancel a job and immediately use its resource, while it is still in Cancelling (running finally). Use cancelAndJoin().

Real-life picture. A restaurant closing: the chef stops cooking (body done) but the restaurant is not closed until every table finishes eating (children).

Common interview traps.

  • Treating "isCompleted" as "succeeded". A cancelled job is also completed.
  • Assuming isActive == false right after cancel() means cleanup finished. It means cancelling started.
  • Forgetting the Completing state exists.

notes.title: Job factory and CompletableJob
notes.html:
The idea. Job() (the function) creates a CompletableJob: a Job with no body. Nobody runs inside it. It is a handle you complete yourself with complete() (success) or completeExceptionally(e) (failure). Both return Boolean (false if already finished). complete() only starts completing: it waits for children, then finishes.

val job = Job()                     // Active, no code attached
scope.launch(job) { work() }        // (anti-pattern, see inheritance section)
job.join()                          // hangs forever unless someone calls job.complete()

Why join() never returns. A coroutine's Job completes when its body ends. A factory Job has no body, so it stays Active until you call complete()/cancel(). With children, complete() + join() is the documented way to "close" a scope and wait.

Where it is legitimately used.

  • CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default): the Job is the scope's lifetime handle.
  • Job(parent) to link a hand-built Job under a parent.
  • Bridging callbacks: val done = CompletableDeferred<Result>() completed from a listener (a CompletableDeferred is the value-carrying cousin).

Industry example. A PlayerManager scope in a video app keeps its SupervisorJob and calls job.complete() / cancel() on release(); Ktor and OkHttp-based sockets use CompletableJob for connection lifetime.

Real-life picture. A meeting room reservation: the room is "booked" until someone presses "release". If nobody does, waiting for it to be free lasts forever.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling join() on Job() without ever completing it.
  • Confusing complete() (graceful, waits for children) with cancel() (stops them).
  • Using Job() where CompletableDeferred was needed to return a value.

notes.title: Parent child contract and Job internals
notes.html:
The contract (three directions).

Direction What happens
Parent waits A parent finishes only after all children finish. parent.join() covers the whole subtree.
Cancel goes down parent.cancel() cancels children.
Failure goes up A child failing (not CancellationException) cancels the parent, which cancels the other children.

A child cancelling normally (a CancellationException) does not cancel the parent: that is how withTimeout, cancel() on a single child and collectLatest work.

job.children is a Sequence<Job> of the currently attached children. Finished children are removed, so it stays small. join() waits for this job and therefore its children.

How it works inside (JobSupport).

  1. Every coroutine is a JobSupport subclass (StandaloneCoroutine, DeferredCoroutine, ScopeCoroutine).
  2. At creation, initParentJob(parent) calls parent.attachChild(this), registering a ChildHandleNode in the parent's internal lock-free list of handlers (NodeList).
  3. Cancel down: when the parent enters Cancelling, it walks its list and calls childJob.parentCancelled(parentJob) for each child.
  4. Fail up: when a child fails, it calls parent.childCancelled(cause). The parent's default implementation returns whether it handled it: it cancels itself with that cause (cancelImpl). If the cause is a CancellationException, the parent ignores it (returns true without cancelling).
  5. SupervisorJob overrides childCancelled to return false (ignores the failure) so the parent stays alive; the exception then goes to the child's own handling: handleJobException, which is the CoroutineExceptionHandler or the thread's uncaught handler. That is exactly why a supervisor child "crashes the app": nobody up the chain absorbs it.
  6. On completion, the child is detached (ChildHandle.dispose()), which prevents a long-living parent from retaining finished children.

Industry example. Debugging a stuck screen: an Activity's lifecycleScope.launch { ... } never ends because one launch inside waits for a never-completed CompletableJob child; coroutine dumps show the parent "Completing".

Real-life picture. A phone chain at a company: when the boss cancels the meeting, he phones each team lead who phones their team (down); if a team lead has a disaster he phones the boss and the boss cancels everything (up), except a boss who has told them "don't bother me".

Common interview traps.

  • Saying failure always cancels the parent. A CancellationException and a SupervisorJob parent do not.
  • Believing the parent holds finished children forever (it removes them).
  • Expecting the SupervisorJob to swallow exceptions: it only stops propagation upward.

notes.title: Scope interface versus scope builders
notes.html:
Three similar names, three different things.

Name What it is Behaviour
interface CoroutineScope A holder of a coroutineContext You implement/hold it so launch has somewhere to attach
CoroutineScope(ctx) factory function Creates a new scope object You own it; nothing waits for it; you must cancel() it
coroutineScope { } A suspend builder Creates a child scope of the current coroutine, runs the block, and suspends until all children finish 
class Repo { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO) }   // factory
suspend fun refresh() = coroutineScope { launch { a() }; launch { b() } }             // builder

The factory adds a Job() for you if the context has none (so it can be cancelled). coroutineScope throws if the block throws and cancels children; it rethrows the exception to the caller (so you can try/catch around it).

The orphan bug. In suspend fun load() { CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch { ... } } the function returns immediately and the work is orphaned. The fix is coroutineScope { launch {...} } (waits) or withContext.

The CoroutineScope receiver on a suspend function. Inside suspend fun CoroutineScope.foo() there are two contexts: the property this.coroutineContext (the scope's) and the suspend-function's own (the calling coroutine's). They may differ. coroutineContext unqualified resolves to the scope receiver's member property (it wins over the top-level kotlin.coroutines.coroutineContext). Use currentCoroutineContext() to get the running one.

Convention. A suspend fun does its work and returns when it is done (callers cancel by cancelling themselves). A non-suspend fun CoroutineScope.foo(): Job (extension on scope) starts work and returns immediately. A function that is both suspend and takes a scope receiver is a smell: it says "I wait" and "I launch things that may outlive me" at the same time, so callers cannot tell whether work is finished. Prefer suspend fun foo() = coroutineScope { ... }.

Real-life picture. CoroutineScope(...) is hiring a new contractor and walking away; coroutineScope { } is a meeting you stay in until everyone is done.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up CoroutineScope(...) and coroutineScope { }.
  • Launching in a fresh CoroutineScope(...) inside a suspend function and expecting it to wait.
  • Not knowing which coroutineContext a scope-receiver suspend function sees.

notes.title: SupervisorJob and supervisorScope
notes.html:
The idea. In a normal tree, one child failing breaks the whole family. A SupervisorJob says: "my children's failures are their own problem; do not cancel me or my other children."

What it changes.

  • A child failure does not cancel the supervisor or siblings (childCancelled returns false).

What it does NOT change.

  • Cancelling the supervisor (or its scope) still cancels all children.
  • Uncaught exceptions still crash the app. No handler means the thread's uncaught exception handler runs. Failed children are not swallowed: install a CoroutineExceptionHandler on the scope (works there because these children are root coroutines) or try/catch inside the child.
  • It applies only to direct children. A grandchild's failure goes up to its parent normally; if that parent is a plain launch, it cancels itself.
  • async children still deliver exceptions through await().
val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO + handler)
scope.launch { uploadA() }     // fails: B continues
scope.launch { uploadB() }

supervisorScope { } versus coroutineScope { }. Both suspend until children finish. coroutineScope: one child fails, siblings are cancelled and the exception is rethrown. supervisorScope: failed children don't affect siblings; the block's own exception still ends the scope; and child exceptions are not rethrown, they go to handlers (so crash unless handled). With async inside, you must await and catch each.

Incident patterns.

  • Analytics uploader: scope built with plain Job() and a periodic launch; one failed batch killed the scope, and every later launch silently did nothing (cancelled scope). Fix: SupervisorJob() plus per-batch try/catch (see the dead-scope section in the exceptions topic).
  • Photo backup: coroutineScope with 50 parallel uploads: the first server-side validation error cancelled the rest ("only 3 uploaded"). Fix: supervisorScope and collect per-photo results (runCatching that rethrows CancellationException), report a summary.
  • Video chat "resilience" PR: wrapping calls in a supervisorScope or SupervisorJob inside long-lived scopes without cancellation tied to the screen leaked work. The policy and ownership are separate decisions.

Industry examples. viewModelScope and lifecycleScope both use SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate; Ktor server's application scope; WorkManager's per-worker scope.

Real-life picture. Each cashier in a supermarket runs their own lane: one cashier's till breaking does not close the other lanes, but if the store closes (cancel), everyone stops.

Common interview traps.

  • "SupervisorJob catches exceptions". It does not.
  • Using launch(SupervisorJob()) instead of a scope with a supervisor.
  • Forgetting the supervisor rule applies only to direct children.

notes.title: Cancelling scopes and cancelChildren
notes.html:
Three cancel tools.

Call Effect Reusable afterwards?
scope.cancel() Cancels the scope's Job (and all children). The Job is now terminal No. Every later launch returns an already-cancelled job and does nothing
scope.coroutineContext.cancelChildren() Cancels children but leaves the scope's own Job active Yes
someJob.cancel() Cancels one coroutine (and its subtree) Scope still works

scope.cancel() throws IllegalStateException("Scope cannot be cancelled because it does not have a job") if the scope has no Job in its context.

When to use which. Screen/ViewModel scopes: cancel() at the end of life (the framework does it). Session scopes that must survive "logout then login": cancelChildren(), or recreate the whole scope. Specific operation (search, refresh): keep a Job reference and cancel it.

The logout incident. sessionScope.coroutineContext.cancelChildren() cancels existing children, but code that started a coroutine outside the tree (via GlobalScope, launch(Job()), another scope, or a thread/Handler/WorkManager task) keeps running. In the banking scenario the transactions prefetch kept firing for up to 20 s, then the interceptor read the cleared token store: NullPointerException. Two fixes: make everything a descendant of the session scope (so cancel reaches it) and order the logout: cancelChildren() followed by join of those children (coroutineContext.job.children.forEach { it.join() }) before clearing tokens; treat a null token as "unauthenticated" with a typed error rather than a crash.

Real-life picture. Switching off one light vs flipping the main breaker: after the breaker, you can't switch lights back on without resetting it.

Common interview traps.

  • Cancelling a scope you wanted to reuse.
  • Assuming cancel() is synchronous. It only requests; the children run finally blocks afterwards.
  • Clearing shared state immediately after cancelChildren() without waiting.

notes.title: Owning custom scopes
notes.html:
When to create one. Framework scopes cover screens (viewModelScope, lifecycleScope). You need your own for things with their own lifetime: an SDK, a download manager, an analytics uploader, a media player, a socket connection, a per-account session.

Rules for a class that owns a scope.

  1. Build it with a Job you control, normally SupervisorJob(), plus an injected dispatcher (testable).
  2. Give the class a close/release/cancel method that cancels the scope; call it from the owner's lifecycle.
  3. Everything the class launches goes into that scope, never GlobalScope.
  4. Don't pass a scope into every repository function (the layered-API smell): each caller then decides lifetimes. Expose suspend functions (caller owns the lifetime) and Flows; keep a scope only where work must outlive the caller.
  5. Provide a CoroutineExceptionHandler for root coroutines.
@Singleton
class SyncManager @Inject constructor(@IoDispatcher io: CoroutineDispatcher) {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + io + CoroutineName("SyncManager"))
    fun start() = scope.launch { ... }
    fun close() = scope.cancel()
}

Application scope via Hilt. The "Now in Android" pattern: an @ApplicationScope qualifier providing a @Singleton CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default), used for must-finish work (e.g. submit payment confirmation).

Layered design (fintech, multi-account).

Application scope  (process life; must-finish work, with its own handler)
   Session scope    (per account; cancelChildren/recreate on switch or logout)
      Screen scope  (viewModelScope / lifecycleScope; dies with the screen)

Work that must survive screen exit goes to the session or application scope (or WorkManager if it must survive process death); screen work stays in viewModelScope.

Replacing GlobalScope (140 call sites). Categorise: (1) UI-bound work to viewModelScope/lifecycleScope; (2) must-finish short work to an injected application scope; (3) deferred/guaranteed work to WorkManager; (4) periodic polling to a lifecycle-aware repeatOnLifecycle. Migrate by category, use Android lint/detekt (GlobalCoroutineUsage) to prevent new ones, and watch OOM/Crashlytics and LeakCanary after rollout. The leaked StandaloneCoroutine objects holding Activities show lambdas capturing this.

Many children in one scope (400k files). Launching one coroutine per item is cheap (hundreds of bytes each) but 400k pending closures plus the file list can add up to tens of MB (here about 90 MB with GC pauses). Bound parallelism: a Channel or flow with flatMapMerge(concurrency), Semaphore, or Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(n); process in batches; or enqueue to WorkManager. Finished children detach, so the leak is pending work, not completed work.

Real-life picture. A shop (class) that hires a delivery crew (scope): the shop must also be able to send them home when it closes.

Common interview traps.

  • A scope field with no cancel() path.
  • Passing a CoroutineScope parameter to every method.
  • Using @Singleton scopes for UI-lifetime work (leaking Activities captured in lambdas).
  • Unbounded launch per item with large collections.

notes.title: Custom context elements
notes.html:
The idea. The context is an extension point: you can carry your own data with a coroutine, such as a request/trace ID, a logging tag, a user session or a feature-flag snapshot, without passing it through every parameter.

data class TraceId(val id: String) : AbstractCoroutineContextElement(TraceId) {
    companion object Key : CoroutineContext.Key<TraceId>
}
scope.launch(TraceId(UUID.randomUUID().toString())) {
    launch { api.call() }   // child inherits TraceId
}
// in an OkHttp interceptor on a suspend caller: currentCoroutineContext()[TraceId]

Propagation rules.

  • Inherited by child coroutines and kept across withContext (unless overridden).
  • Not propagated into plain threads, Executor.execute, Handler.post, callbacks, or WorkManager workers. You must copy it yourself.
  • flow { } emission respects context preservation: a flowOn changes the upstream context but keeps your elements unless you override the key.
  • A ThreadContextElement (for ThreadLocals such as MDC logging or StrictMode-style state) sets/restores the thread-local each time the coroutine resumes on a thread; it costs on every resume, so keep it light.
  • Elements should be immutable; a mutable element is shared by all children (race conditions).

Pitfalls. Forgetting that two elements with the same Key replace each other; putting heavy objects (Activity, Context) into the context (leak); assuming the value is visible in Retrofit's OkHttp interceptor thread (it isn't; OkHttp's dispatcher uses its own threads). Pass it as a header at the suspend boundary instead.

Industry examples. Ktor's CallLogging MDC, Sentry/Datadog trace propagation, Spring/Reactor-Kotlin interop, Apollo Kotlin's execution context.

Real-life picture. A luggage tag that follows the suitcase through every belt, as long as it stays on the airport's conveyor system; a different system (taxi) doesn't read the tag.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting a context element to be visible in a callback thread.
  • Making an element mutable or storing an Activity in it.
  • Using a class without a Key companion (the default key becomes the class's own type only when you write it so).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Structured concurrency = a parent outlives its children, cancellation goes down, failures go up.
  • The context is an immutable keyed map; + is right-biased; each coroutine gets a fresh Job whose parent is the Job in the computed context.
  • launch(Job())/launch(SupervisorJob()) detaches work from the scope: always a bug.
  • Job states: Completing and Cancelling are real; isCompleted is true for cancelled jobs too; Job() has no body, so join() needs complete().
  • SupervisorJob only stops upward propagation from direct children; it does not catch exceptions and does not stop downward cancellation.
  • scope.cancel() kills the scope for good; cancelChildren() doesn't. Wait for children before clearing shared state.
  • Scope owners need an injected dispatcher, a SupervisorJob and a close path; prefer suspend functions over passing scopes around.
  • Custom context elements travel only along the coroutine tree, not across raw threads or callbacks.

questions.promptHtml: What is structured concurrency, and what does it actually guarantee you in kotlinx.coroutines?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Everything else (scopes, Job, SupervisorJob, viewModelScope) builds on it. Candidates who can only say "coroutines are lightweight threads" haven't understood the model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Structured concurrency means every coroutine starts inside a scope and becomes a child of that scope's Job, so coroutines form a tree. That tree gives three guarantees. A parent doesn't complete until all its children complete. Cancelling a parent cancels every descendant. A child that fails with a real exception cancels its parent, and therefore its siblings, so errors can't be silently lost. Put simply, the lifetime of concurrent work is bound to a lexical block or an owning object, the same way a local variable's lifetime is bound to its block.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Before structured concurrency, the common model was "fire a thread/Future and hope someone keeps a reference to it". Three problems followed:

  1. Leaks: work outlives whoever needed it (a network call keeps running after the screen is gone).
  2. Lost errors: an exception in a background task goes nowhere, or crashes an unrelated thread.
  3. No clean cancellation: cancelling "the operation" means tracking every Future by hand.

kotlinx.coroutines fixes this by making the Job hierarchy the source of truth:

viewModelScope (SupervisorJob)
 ├── launch { loadFeed() }            Job A
 │     ├── async { api.posts() }      Job A1
 │     └── async { api.stories() }    Job A2
 └── launch { observeUser() }         Job B
Guarantee Mechanism What it means at runtime
Parent waits for children Parent enters the Completing state after its body finishes, and only becomes Completed once all children are final coroutineScope { launch{}; launch{} } returns only after both launches finish
Cancellation flows down Parent cancellation is pushed to every attached child (recursively) viewModelScope cancelled in onCleared() → A, A1, A2, B all get CancellationException at their next suspension point
Failure flows up A child failing with a non-CancellationException notifies the parent, which cancels itself and the remaining children (unless the parent is a supervisor) A1 throws IOException → A is cancelled → A2 is cancelled → the exception surfaces at A
No lost exceptions The exception lands in exactly one place: the parent, await(), or (at the root) a CoroutineExceptionHandler / the uncaught handler You can't "forget" a failure the way you can with an unobserved Future

Structured concurrency is a convention enforced by the API shape. launch/async are extensions on CoroutineScope, so you need a scope to start anything, and suspending scope builders (coroutineScope, supervisorScope, withContext) make suspending functions finish all their concurrent work before returning. You can opt out with GlobalScope, a fresh Job() passed into launch, or a scope you never cancel. Opting out is exactly where most production bugs come from.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Structured: returns only when both requests finish; if one fails, the other is cancelled.
suspend fun loadDashboard(): Dashboard = coroutineScope {
    val profile = async { api.profile() }
    val feed = async { api.feed() }
    Dashboard(profile.await(), feed.await())
}

// Unstructured: returns immediately, work is orphaned, failure is reported nowhere useful.
fun loadDashboardBroken() {
    GlobalScope.launch { api.profile() }   // no owner, no cancellation, no parent
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking structured concurrency is about threads. It's about lifetimes and error propagation, and it's independent of the dispatcher.
  • Believing "child failure cancels the parent" applies to CancellationException. It doesn't; cancellation is treated as normal completion for propagation purposes.
  • Assuming viewModelScope follows the default failure rule. It's built on a SupervisorJob, so one failed launch doesn't kill its siblings.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens to children when the parent's body finishes first? → The parent stays in Completing (still isActive == true to observers) until every child is done.
  2. How do you deliberately break structure? → GlobalScope, launch(Job()), or launching into some other long-lived scope. Each needs a written justification.
  3. Does structured concurrency guarantee a cancelled coroutine stops immediately? → No. Cancellation is cooperative; it only takes effect at suspension points or explicit checks (covered in the cancellation section).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "Coroutines are launched in a scope and are cancelled when the scope is cancelled." The senior answer names all three directions (wait, cancel-down, fail-up), connects them to the Job tree and the Completing state, and points out that the guarantees vanish the moment someone injects a foreign Job or uses a scope nobody owns.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The most common "zombie request" bugs (uploads continuing after logout, analytics firing after a screen closes) trace back to one coroutine being launched outside the tree, which means outside every guarantee above.

questions.promptHtml: What is a CoroutineContext? What elements does it typically hold, and how do you read one?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Dispatchers, Jobs, names and exception handlers all reach a coroutine through the context. If you don't understand it, the inheritance rules will look like magic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A CoroutineContext is an immutable, indexed set of elements, keyed by type. Each element has a unique Key. The usual ones are a Job (lifecycle), a ContinuationInterceptor, which in practice means a CoroutineDispatcher (where code runs), a CoroutineName (debug label), and a CoroutineExceptionHandler. You read an element with the index operator, coroutineContext[Job] or coroutineContext[CoroutineName], and combine contexts with +. Every coroutine carries one, and children derive theirs from the parent's.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Think of a context as a Map<Key, Element> with two twists:

  • Each element is itself a context (Element : CoroutineContext), so Dispatchers.IO alone is a valid one-element context, and Dispatchers.IO + CoroutineName("sync") is a two-element context.
  • The key is usually the companion object of the element's class. That's why context[Job] works: Job here refers to Job.Key.
CoroutineContext of a launch inside viewModelScope:
┌──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┐
│ Key                      │ Element                           │
├──────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
│ Job                      │ StandaloneCoroutine{Active}@1a2b  │  ← the coroutine itself
│ ContinuationInterceptor  │ Dispatchers.Main.immediate        │
│ CoroutineName (optional) │ CoroutineName(feed)               │
│ CoroutineExceptionHandler│ (only if you added one)           │
└──────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘

Core API (from kotlin.coroutines, stdlib):

API Meaning
operator fun <E : Element> get(key: Key<E>): E? Look up an element or get null
operator fun plus(context) Merge; on a key clash the right-hand side wins
fun minusKey(key) Context without that key
fun <R> fold(initial, op) Iterate over elements
EmptyCoroutineContext The identity element for +

Inside a coroutine you get the context from coroutineContext: the property on the CoroutineScope receiver, or the top-level suspend property in suspend functions (the difference matters, see Q341). currentCoroutineContext() is the unambiguous way to read it in suspend code. The coroutineContext.job extension returns the Job or throws IllegalStateException if there is none, while coroutineContext[Job] returns null.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun whereAmI() {
    val ctx = currentCoroutineContext()
    val name = ctx[CoroutineName]?.name ?: "unnamed"
    val dispatcher = ctx[ContinuationInterceptor]
    val job = ctx.job               // throws if no Job (unusual inside a real coroutine)
    Log.d("Ctx", "name=$name dispatcher=$dispatcher active=${job.isActive}")
}

val ctx: CoroutineContext = Dispatchers.IO + CoroutineName("sync")  // two elements

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating the context as mutable. + returns a new context; the old one is unchanged.
  • Calling ctx[CoroutineDispatcher]. That works because CoroutineDispatcher has a polymorphic key, but ContinuationInterceptor is the canonical key, and both refer to the same slot.
  • Thinking CoroutineExceptionHandler in a child's context does anything. It's inherited but only consulted at the root (covered in the exception-handling section).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is a single dispatcher a valid context? → Every Element implements CoroutineContext; a single element is a one-entry set.
  2. Can a context contain two dispatchers? → No. They share the ContinuationInterceptor key, so the later one replaces the earlier.
  3. What does EmptyCoroutineContext + x return? → x itself. Empty is the identity, so no wrapper is allocated.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "it holds the dispatcher and the job". The senior answer describes it as a keyed, immutable set of elements that are themselves contexts, knows the right-wins + rule and minusKey, and knows which elements are inherited and which (the Job) are always replaced for a new coroutine.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams wanting request-level correlation IDs in logs implement them as a custom context element (Q342). That only works if engineers know the context propagates to children automatically and doesn't cross into a foreign scope.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the states of a Job. What do isActive, isCompleted and isCancelled return in each one?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you know that "finished body" and "completed job" are different, which is the root of many join/wait bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Job starts as New (only with CoroutineStart.LAZY) or Active (the default). When its body finishes it moves to Completing and waits for its children, then becomes Completed. If it fails or is cancelled, it moves to Cancelling while children and finally blocks wind down, then becomes Cancelled. Observers see Completing as still active. isCompleted is true for both final states, and isCancelled is true from Cancelling onward, including when the job failed with a real exception.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
State table (from the kotlinx.coroutines Job KDoc):

State isActive isCompleted isCancelled
New (optional initial) false false false
Active (default initial) true false false
Completing (transient) true false false
Cancelling (transient) false false true
Cancelled (final) false true true
Completed (final) false true false 
                    wait children
  +-----+ start +--------+ body done +------------+  all children +-----------+
  | New | ----> | Active | --------> | Completing | ------------> | Completed |
  +-----+       +--------+           +------------+     done      +-----------+
                    |  cancel / fail       |
                    v                      v
               +------------+   all children done   +-----------+
               | Cancelling | --------------------> | Cancelled |
               +------------+   + finally blocks    +-----------+

Key behaviours:

  • New → Active happens on start() or join(), and also on await() for a lazy async.
  • Completing is invisible from outside: isActive is still true. A parent whose code has returned but whose children are still running reports active.
  • "Failed" is not a separate state. A job that failed with an exception goes through Cancelling to Cancelled, and the exception becomes its cancellation cause. You tell failure from cancellation by the cause, for example in invokeOnCompletion { cause -> }: null means success, a CancellationException means cancelled, anything else means failure.
  • Cancelling can take time. A non-cooperative child or a long withContext(NonCancellable) in a finally keeps the job in Cancelling, which is why cancelAndJoin() exists.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun main() = runBlocking {
    val job = launch(start = CoroutineStart.LAZY) { delay(1_000) }
    println(job.isActive)          // false (New)
    job.start()
    println(job.isActive)          // true  (Active)
    job.invokeOnCompletion { cause -> println("done, cause=$cause") }
    job.cancelAndJoin()
    println("${job.isCancelled} ${job.isCompleted}") // true true (Cancelled)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using !isActive to mean "finished". A New lazy job is also !isActive, and so is a Cancelling job whose cleanup is still running. Use isCompleted or join().
  • Expecting isCancelled == false for a job that crashed. Failure is a form of cancellation.
  • Polling state flags in a loop instead of suspending on join().

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does join() throw if the job failed? → No. join resumes normally whatever the outcome; only await() on a Deferred rethrows. join throws CancellationException only if the caller is cancelled.
  2. How do I learn why a job ended? → invokeOnCompletion { cause -> }, or getCancellationException() while it's cancelling or cancelled.
  3. Why does the Completing state exist? → To implement "parent waits for children" without blocking a thread: the body is done, but completion is deferred until the child count reaches zero.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate lists Active, Cancelled and Completed. A senior adds the two transient states, explains why Completing looks active, treats failure as cancellation with a non-CancellationException cause, and uses that knowledge to avoid state-polling bugs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "sync finished" indicator driven by job.isActive == false flashed "done" while cleanup was still writing to the DB in Cancelling. Switching to invokeOnCompletion fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: What's the difference between the CoroutineScope interface, the CoroutineScope(...) factory function, and the coroutineScope { } builder?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Three things share almost the same name. Mixing them up leads to orphaned coroutines and to suspend functions that return before their work is done.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CoroutineScope is just an interface with one property, coroutineContext. It's the receiver that launch and async need. CoroutineScope(context) is a factory that builds a standalone scope object and adds a Job() if you didn't pass one. You use it for a component that owns work, and that component must cancel it. coroutineScope { } is a suspending builder: it creates a child scope of the current coroutine, runs the block, waits for every child, and rethrows failures. It's how a suspend function does parallel work without leaking it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
interface CoroutineScope CoroutineScope(ctx) factory coroutineScope { } builder
What it is Contract: val coroutineContext: CoroutineContext Function returning a CoroutineScope suspend fun <R> coroutineScope(block: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> R): R
Job Whatever the implementer provides (possibly none!) Adds Job() if ctx lacks one New child Job of the caller's Job
Lifetime Defined by its owner Until someone calls cancel() Until the block and all its children finish
Suspends caller? n/a No Yes, until all children are done
Failure n/a Child failure cancels the scope (unless you used SupervisorJob) Child failure cancels siblings and is rethrown to the caller
Typical use viewModelScope, lifecycleScope implement it Class-owned scope in a manager/service Parallel decomposition in a suspend function

MainScope() is a sibling factory: SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.

The convention that ties them together:

  • A suspend function does all its work before returning. If it needs concurrency, it uses coroutineScope {}.
  • A function that starts work and returns immediately should be an extension on CoroutineScope, or take an explicit scope, so the caller sees from the signature that work outlives the call.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Uploader(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher) {
    // Factory: owned scope. Job is added automatically; we pass SupervisorJob to isolate uploads.
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher)

    fun enqueue(file: File) { scope.launch { upload(file) } }   // returns immediately
    fun shutdown() = scope.cancel()

    // Builder: suspends until both parts are uploaded; a failure cancels the other and is rethrown.
    private suspend fun upload(file: File) = coroutineScope {
        val meta = async { api.uploadMeta(file) }
        val body = async { api.uploadBody(file) }
        meta.await(); body.await()
    }
}

// BROKEN: an anonymous CoroutineScope with no Job. launch works, but scope.cancel() throws
// IllegalStateException("Scope cannot be cancelled because it does not have a job").
val badScope = object : CoroutineScope { override val coroutineContext = Dispatchers.IO }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch { } inline inside a function. It creates a new root scope on every call that nobody can cancel, which is GlobalScope by another name.
  • Implementing CoroutineScope by hand without a Job.
  • Using coroutineScope {} and expecting it to return early. It always waits for its children.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. coroutineScope vs withContext? → Both create a child scope and wait. withContext also changes context elements such as the dispatcher (builders section).
  2. coroutineScope vs supervisorScope? → Same, except a child failure doesn't cancel siblings or the scope (Q336).
  3. Why does the factory add a Job automatically? → So cancel() and structured children work. Without a Job, children have no parent and the scope can't be cancelled.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average candidate knows coroutineScope {} waits. The senior can tell all three apart in one sentence each, knows the factory's auto-Job behaviour and the "cannot be cancelled" failure, and enforces the suspend-vs-CoroutineScope-extension signature convention in reviews.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A helper fun fetchAsync() = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch { ... } was copied across a codebase. Each call created an unowned root, and logout couldn't stop any of them.

questions.promptHtml: What is CoroutineName for, and how do you actually see it at runtime on Android?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's a cheap debugging tool that shows whether you've debugged real concurrent code or only written it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CoroutineName is a context element that labels a coroutine for debugging. Children inherit it unless they override it. It doesn't change behaviour. You see it in the coroutine's toString(), in DebugProbes dumps and in the IDE coroutine debugger, and with debug mode on (system property kotlinx.coroutines.debug), the thread name gets suffixed with @name#id while the coroutine runs. On Android, debug mode isn't on by default, so you enable it explicitly in debug builds.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Definition: data class CoroutineName(val name: String) : AbstractCoroutineContextElement(CoroutineName). It's a plain element with key CoroutineName.Key.
  • Inheritance: Like every non-Job element, it's copied into child contexts. launch(CoroutineName("child")) overrides it for that subtree.
  • Debug mode: On the JVM, debug mode turns on with -Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug or automatically when JVM assertions are enabled (-ea). Android doesn't run with -ea, so set System.setProperty(DEBUG_PROPERTY_NAME, DEBUG_PROPERTY_VALUE_ON) very early (for example in Application.onCreate, debug builds only). With it on, each coroutine gets an ID, and the thread name becomes something like DefaultDispatcher-worker-3 @image-decode#42 for the time that coroutine is running on it.
  • Cost: The name itself costs one small allocation. Debug mode adds a per-coroutine ID and thread-rename work on each resume, so keep it off in release.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FeedViewModel : ViewModel() {
    fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch(CoroutineName("feed-refresh")) {
        val posts = async(CoroutineName("posts")) { repo.posts() }
        val ads = async { repo.ads() }           // inherits "feed-refresh"
        render(posts.await(), ads.await())
    }
}

// Debug builds only:
if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) System.setProperty(DEBUG_PROPERTY_NAME, DEBUG_PROPERTY_VALUE_ON)
// Log.d(TAG, Thread.currentThread().name) -> "DefaultDispatcher-worker-2 @posts#17"

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting the name in thread names without enabling debug mode.
  • Enabling debug mode in release builds and paying the overhead for nothing.
  • Using CoroutineName as business data. Use a dedicated custom element for that (Q342).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a child inherit the parent's name? → Yes, unless it passes its own CoroutineName.
  2. Where else does it help? → DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() and the Android Studio coroutine debugger (debugging section).
  3. Can I add a name to an existing scope? → Scopes are immutable. Use scope + CoroutineName("x") (CoroutineScope.plus) to get a new scope object that shares the same Job.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer: "it gives a coroutine a name". The senior explains inheritance, the debug-mode requirement on Android, and the overhead trade-off, and names coroutines on hot paths so an incident dump can be read.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: In a starvation investigation, naming the coroutines in the image pipeline made a debug-build thread dump show that all 64 IO workers were @thumbnail#..., which identified the culprit in minutes.

questions.promptHtml: Explain exactly how + works on CoroutineContext. What happens on key collisions, what does minusKey do, and how are keys defined?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Override-order bugs ("why is this running on Main?") and custom element design both depend on it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: a + b produces a context with all elements of both. When the same key appears on both sides, the element from b, the right-hand side, wins. minusKey(k) returns the context without that key. Keys are usually companion objects implementing CoroutineContext.Key<E>, so ctx[Job] reads naturally. Dispatchers use a polymorphic key, AbstractCoroutineContextKey, so both ctx[ContinuationInterceptor] and ctx[CoroutineDispatcher] find the same element. The implementation is a small immutable linked structure, and the interceptor is deliberately kept at the end so dispatch lookups are fast.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Stdlib behaviour of plus:

  1. If the right side is EmptyCoroutineContext, return the left unchanged.
  2. Fold the right-side elements into the left: for each element, remove any existing element with the same key from the accumulator, then append the new element.
  3. The ContinuationInterceptor is re-positioned to the outermost node of the resulting CombinedContext, so get(ContinuationInterceptor), which runs on every dispatch, is O(1).
(Dispatchers.Main + CoroutineName("a")) + (CoroutineName("b") + Dispatchers.IO)
= { Name("b"), IO }                      // both keys clashed; right side won each time

So contexts are ordered sets with last-writer-wins semantics, much like mapA + mapB in Kotlin.

Keys:

public interface Job : CoroutineContext.Element {
    public companion object Key : CoroutineContext.Key<Job>
    ...
}

The companion-object-as-key trick makes context[Job] type-safe and returns Job?.

Polymorphic keys: CoroutineDispatcher has a key declared as AbstractCoroutineContextKey<ContinuationInterceptor, CoroutineDispatcher>, which means "my base key is ContinuationInterceptor". A context therefore holds at most one interceptor, and you can look it up through either key. If you write a custom element hierarchy, the same pattern is available via @ExperimentalStdlibApi APIs (AbstractCoroutineContextKey, getPolymorphicElement). Check its experimental status for your Kotlin version before relying on it.

minusKey: ctx.minusKey(Job) is the idiomatic way to strip a Job when you want to copy the settings of a context (dispatcher, name) into a new independent scope without linking lifetimes.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val base = Dispatchers.Main + CoroutineName("ui")
val io = base + Dispatchers.IO                    // IO replaces Main; name kept
check(io[ContinuationInterceptor] == Dispatchers.IO)

// Copy settings, not lifetime: build a scope that is independent of the caller's Job.
suspend fun detachedSettings(): CoroutineContext = currentCoroutineContext().minusKey(Job)

// Order matters: the caller's argument should come last if it is meant to override defaults.
fun CoroutineScope.launchTracked(ctx: CoroutineContext = EmptyCoroutineContext, block: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit) =
    launch(CoroutineName("tracked") + ctx, block = block)    // caller's name wins if given

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing ctx + defaults when you meant defaults + ctx, so the defaults silently override the caller's choice.
  • Assuming + on a scope (scope + Dispatchers.IO) creates a child scope. It creates a new scope object that shares the same Job; cancelling either cancels both.
  • Defining a custom element without a companion Key, so every instance has a different key and they accumulate instead of replacing each other.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is + commutative? → No. On clashing keys, the order decides which element wins.
  2. What does fold give you? → Iteration over the elements. Used internally, for example to copy CopyableThreadContextElements to children.
  3. Why keep the interceptor at a fixed position? → Every resume looks up the dispatcher; keeping it at the head of the combined structure avoids a list walk on a hot path.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "plus combines contexts, right one wins." The senior also covers polymorphic keys, why there can be only one dispatcher, minusKey(Job) as the tool for copying settings without lifetime, and the trap that scope + x shares the Job.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A wrapper launchOnIo(ctx) = launch(ctx + Dispatchers.IO) meant callers who passed Dispatchers.Main for a UI-touching block still ran on IO. Order mattered, and it crashed with CalledFromWrongThreadException.

questions.promptHtml: When I call scope.launch(ctx) { }, how exactly is the new coroutine's context computed? Which elements are inherited and which are always new?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This is the precise mechanism behind both the "default dispatcher" surprise and the launch(Job()) bug.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The parent context is the scope's context plus whatever I pass, with my argument winning on clashes. If the result has no dispatcher, Dispatchers.Default is added. In debug mode, a coroutine ID is added too. Then the new coroutine creates its own Job, a child of whatever Job is in that parent context, and its final context is the parent context plus its own Job. So the dispatcher, name and handler are inherited or overridden, but the Job is never inherited as-is. It's always a fresh child Job whose parent is the Job found in the combined context.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Simplified from newCoroutineContext and AbstractCoroutine in kotlinx.coroutines:

1. combined     = scope.coroutineContext + ctxArgument       (right wins)
2. if combined has no ContinuationInterceptor → combined += Dispatchers.Default
3. if debug mode → combined += CoroutineId(nextId)
4. newCoroutine = StandaloneCoroutine(parentContext = combined)   // it IS a Job
5. newCoroutine attaches as child of combined[Job]               // parent link
6. newCoroutine.context = combined + newCoroutine                // its own Job replaces the parent's in its context

Consequences:

Element in combined context Effect on the child
Scope's Job (normal case) The child's parent is the scope's Job. Structured.
Job you passed in ctx (launch(Job())) Your Job becomes the parent and the scope's Job is ignored (Q337)
NonCancellable (a special Job) The parent is a Job that never cancels, so the child is detached from cancellation. That's correct inside withContext in a finally, wrong in launch
Dispatcher Inherited unless overridden. If absent everywhere: Default
CoroutineName / CoroutineExceptionHandler / custom elements Inherited unless overridden
CopyableThreadContextElement Copied per child via copyForChild()/mergeForChild() (since 1.6). Most elements are shared by reference

async, withContext, coroutineScope and supervisorScope follow the same rule. The scope builders always create a child of the current coroutine's Job, while withContext(ctx) creates a child of ctx[Job] if you pass one.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main + CoroutineName("screen"))

scope.launch {                             // Main, name "screen", parent = SupervisorJob
    launch(Dispatchers.IO) { }             // IO, name "screen", parent = outer launch's Job
    launch(CoroutineName("img")) { }       // Main, name "img"
}

CoroutineScope(EmptyCoroutineContext).launch {
    // No dispatcher anywhere → Dispatchers.Default (not Main!)
}

scope.launch(Job()) { }                    // parent = the new Job(), NOT the scope (bug)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing "child inherits the parent's Job". It inherits the parent link, but gets its own Job.
  • Building CoroutineScope(Job()) and being surprised its coroutines run on Default.
  • Assuming a CoroutineExceptionHandler inherited by a child will be used there. It's ignored except at the root.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is coroutineContext[Job] inside launch? → The launched coroutine itself. StandaloneCoroutine implements Job.
  2. What is the parent of withContext(Dispatchers.IO)'s coroutine? → The calling coroutine's Job, because withContext merges the caller's context, which has the caller's Job.
  3. Can a child have two parents? → No. One Job slot means one parent, which is why injecting a Job replaces the scope link instead of adding to it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "children inherit the parent's context." The senior gives the four-step computation, says the Job is always new and parented by whatever Job is in the merged context, and derives the Default fallback and the launch(Job()) bug from that one rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A library exposed fun start(context: CoroutineContext = EmptyCoroutineContext) and internally did scope.launch(context). A caller passed coroutineContext from another component, which contained that component's Job. The library's work then became a child of the wrong lifecycle and was cancelled whenever the other screen closed.

questions.promptHtml: Describe the parent-child contract between Jobs: what a parent waits for, what flows in which direction, and how join() and children fit in.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most coroutine bugs are misunderstandings of this contract. Getting the directions right separates people who have read the docs from people who have debugged with them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The contract has three rules. Downward: cancelling a parent cancels all its children, recursively. Upward: a child that fails with a non-CancellationException cancels its parent, which then cancels the other children, unless the parent is a SupervisorJob. A child that's merely cancelled doesn't affect the parent. Waiting: a parent only reaches a final state after all its children have. join() suspends until a job is final, whatever the outcome, and doesn't throw on the child's failure. children gives me the current direct children as a Sequence, which is mainly useful for debugging or targeted waits.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Parent (Job)
        cancel ↓          ↑ fail (non-CancellationException)
   ┌────────────┼────────────┐
 Child A     Child B      Child C
   │ cancelled: parent NOT affected
   │ failed:    parent cancels → B, C cancelled → parent completes exceptionally
Event Default Job parent SupervisorJob parent
Parent cancelled All children cancelled All children cancelled
Child cancelled (CancellationException) Nothing else happens Nothing else happens
Child fails (other exception) Parent + siblings cancelled; exception propagates up Only that child ends; exception goes to the child's handler / uncaught handler
Parent body finishes Parent waits (Completing) for children Same

join():

  • Suspends until the job is Completed or Cancelled.
  • Doesn't rethrow the job's exception. Use Deferred.await() for results and errors.
  • Throws CancellationException if the caller is cancelled while waiting.
  • Starts a lazy (New) job.
  • joinAll(jobs) / Collection<Job>.joinAll() waits for several.

children: job.children: Sequence<Job> is a live snapshot of direct, still-attached children. Completed children detach themselves, so the sequence shrinks over time. Use it for diagnostics ("how many uploads are in flight?") or job.children.forEach { it.join() }. Don't use it as a registry for business logic.

parent: Job.parent exists but is marked experimental and returns null for a root job or one that has completed. Don't build logic on it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun main() = runBlocking {
    val parent = launch {
        launch { delay(100); println("A done") }
        launch { delay(200); println("B done") }
        println("parent body done")          // prints first; parent now Completing
    }
    parent.join()                            // waits for A and B too
    println("parent final")

    val failing = launch(SupervisorJob()) {  // detached on purpose for demo only (see Q337)
        throw IOException("boom")
    }
    failing.join()                           // does NOT throw; exception went to the uncaught handler
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping job.join() in try/catch to catch the job's failure. That never fires for the child's exception.
  • Assuming a cancelled child cancels the parent. Only failures propagate upward.
  • Iterating children and treating it as stable while children are completing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A child is stuck in a non-cancellable loop. Does the parent complete? → No. The parent stays in Cancelling until that child finishes; the tree waits on its slowest member.
  2. Difference between job.cancelAndJoin() and job.cancel(); job.join()? → Same behaviour; the first is a convenience.
  3. How does failure-up interact with async? → An async child that fails cancels its parent immediately in a regular scope, even if nobody ever calls await() (covered in the exception-handling section).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer: "cancelling the parent cancels the children." The senior states all three directions, the cancellation-vs-failure asymmetry, what join does and doesn't throw, and that a single non-cooperative child keeps the whole tree in Cancelling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "Cancel sync" button hung the UI spinner for 30 s because cancelAndJoin() was waiting on one child doing a blocking SQLite batch with no cancellation checks. The tree was correct; one leaf wasn't cooperative.

questions.promptHtml: What exactly does a SupervisorJob change, and what does it not change? How is supervisorScope different from coroutineScope?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "Use SupervisorJob so one failure doesn't kill the others" is a memorized line. Interviewers check whether you know its limits: still cancellable from above, uncaught exceptions still crash, it only applies to direct children.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A SupervisorJob changes one rule: a failing child doesn't cancel the supervisor or its siblings. Everything else stays the same. Cancelling the supervisor still cancels all children, it still waits for children, and the failed child's exception still has to go somewhere. For a launch child, that's a CoroutineExceptionHandler in its context or the thread's uncaught handler, which crashes an Android app. Supervision only applies to direct children; grandchildren under a regular Job still fail their parent normally. supervisorScope {} is the suspending builder with those semantics: children are isolated, but if the block's own code throws, the scope fails and rethrows like coroutineScope.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Internally, when a child fails it asks its parent to handle it (childCancelled(cause)). A regular Job answers "yes, I'll cancel myself". A supervisor answers "no", so the child must deal with the exception itself (Q343).

supervisorScope {                         SupervisorJob
    launch { A() }         ── fails ──►   A ends; B, C keep running
    launch { B() }                        exception → CEH or uncaught handler
    launch {                              C (regular Job inside)
        launch { C1() }    ── fails ──►   C1 fails → C cancelled → C2 cancelled
        launch { C2() }                   (supervision did not reach this level)
    }
}
Aspect coroutineScope supervisorScope
Child failure Cancels siblings + scope; rethrown from the builder Only that child ends
Where the child's exception goes Up to the caller launch: CEH from the child's context, else uncaught handler. async: stored in the Deferred, thrown on await()
Block itself throws Rethrown, children cancelled Rethrown, children cancelled (same)
External cancellation Cancels all Cancels all (same)
Waits for children Yes Yes

SupervisorJob(parent) accepts an optional parent, so you can build a supervisor that is still a child of a larger lifetime. Example: SupervisorJob(appScope.coroutineContext.job) for a per-session scope.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Correct: independent widgets; each failure handled locally.
suspend fun loadWidgets(): List<WidgetState> = supervisorScope {
    widgetIds.map { id ->
        async { runCatchingNonCancellation { repo.widget(id) } }   // handle per child
    }.awaitAll()
}

// Helper that rethrows cancellation instead of swallowing it.
suspend inline fun <T> runCatchingNonCancellation(block: () -> T): Result<T> =
    try { Result.success(block()) } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { Result.failure(e) }

// Trap: supervisorScope + launch with no handler. A failure here still crashes the app.
suspend fun fireAll() = supervisorScope {
    launch { error("unhandled") }   // → Thread.UncaughtExceptionHandler → process crash on Android
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing SupervisorJob "catches" exceptions. It only stops propagation; the exception is still uncaught unless you handle it.
  • async under a supervisor, then awaitAll() without handling. awaitAll rethrows the first failure, and the caller fails anyway.
  • Expecting supervision at every level of nesting.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does viewModelScope use a SupervisorJob? → So one failed launch (say, an analytics call) doesn't cancel unrelated work on the same screen.
  2. Can I write supervisorScope as withContext(SupervisorJob())? → No. That makes the new Job the parent and breaks the link to the caller (Q337).
  3. If a supervisor's child fails, is the supervisor's isCancelled true? → No. It stays Active.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "SupervisorJob stops one child's failure from cancelling the others." The senior adds: still cancellable from above, exceptions still need a handler or they crash, only direct children are covered, the block's own failure still propagates, and supervisorScope is the structured way to get it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team switched to supervisorScope to "stop crashes" during a home-screen load and turned partial failures into process crashes, because the launch children had no handler. Catching inside each child was the actual fix.

questions.promptHtml: Why is scope.launch(SupervisorJob()) { ... } (or launch(Job())) a bug? What does it actually do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's one of the most common coroutine anti-patterns in real codebases, and an easy signal of whether a candidate understands context inheritance rather than reciting rules.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The Job you pass becomes the new coroutine's parent, replacing the scope's Job. So the coroutine is no longer a child of the scope. Cancelling the scope, say viewModelScope in onCleared, doesn't cancel it. The scope doesn't wait for it. And the "supervision" people wanted is pointless, because the new SupervisorJob has exactly one child and nothing else to protect. Worse, that fresh Job is never completed, so it stays Active forever. The kotlinx.coroutines KDoc for launch now explicitly calls passing a Job an unsupported pattern that breaks structured concurrency. The fix is supervisorScope {}, or handling the exception inside the child.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Using the inheritance rule from Q334:

viewModelScope.launch(SupervisorJob()) { work() }

combined context = viewModelScope.ctx + SupervisorJob()   // right side wins the Job key
                 = { Main.immediate, SupervisorJob#new }
new coroutine parent = SupervisorJob#new                  // NOT viewModelScope's job

viewModelScope.Job ──X── (no link)
SupervisorJob#new ── child: work()

What the developer usually intended and what actually happened:

Intent Reality
"Make this coroutine's failure not cancel siblings" viewModelScope is already a supervisor. If the scope were a plain Job, the right tool is supervisorScope or try/catch
"Isolate failures among this coroutine's own children" Possible, but its children are isolated from each other and the whole subtree is detached from cancellation
"Still be cancelled when the screen closes" Lost. It survives onCleared()

The same applies to async(Job()), withContext(Job()) and withContext(SupervisorJob()). The single legitimate member of this family is withContext(NonCancellable) in cleanup code. That one is deliberately detached, short, and awaited by the caller.

If you really must create a separate Job that keeps the parent link, pass the parent explicitly: Job(parent = coroutineContext.job). Then remember to complete() it. This is almost never worth the confusion; a scope builder is clearer.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// BROKEN: survives onCleared(); scope can't cancel or await it.
fun syncBroken() = viewModelScope.launch(SupervisorJob()) {
    repo.syncEverything()
}

// CORRECT: isolate the children's failures, stay inside the tree.
fun sync() = viewModelScope.launch {
    supervisorScope {
        launch { repo.syncContacts() }
        launch { repo.syncPhotos() }
    }
}

// CORRECT, if you only need to stop this one failure from escaping:
fun syncOne() = viewModelScope.launch {
    try { repo.syncEverything() }
    catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
    catch (e: IOException) { _state.update { it.copy(error = e.message) } }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Fixing" a crash by adding SupervisorJob() to launch. It doesn't catch anything; with no handler, the exception still reaches the uncaught handler.
  • Code review blindness: launch(Dispatchers.IO + SupervisorJob()) reads like a dispatcher choice.
  • Adding CoroutineExceptionHandler and SupervisorJob() together "to be safe". The handler works, because this coroutine is now a root, but the leak remains.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you catch this automatically? → Static analysis. Sonar's Kotlin rule S6306 flags passing Job()/SupervisorJob() to builders. A custom lint/detekt rule on launch/async/withContext arguments of type Job also works.
  2. Is CoroutineScope(coroutineContext + SupervisorJob()) the same bug? → Yes. A new root scope that is no longer cancelled by the caller.
  3. When is detaching legitimate? → Work that must outlive the caller belongs in an explicitly owned longer-lived scope (app/session scope), not in an anonymous Job.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer often recommends launch(SupervisorJob()). The senior derives the bug from "the Job in the merged context becomes the parent", lists the three lost guarantees, notes the never-completing Job, offers supervisorScope/try-catch, and suggests a lint rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After users navigated away, a "sync" coroutine launched with SupervisorJob() kept writing to a Room DB that the next screen was also writing to. The duplicate rows were traced to two copies of the same detached sync running concurrently.

questions.promptHtml: What's the difference between scope.cancel(), scope.coroutineContext.cancelChildren(), and cancelling an individual Job? When do you use each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A cancelled scope is dead forever. Using cancel() where cancelChildren() was needed is a classic "nothing works after logout" bug.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: scope.cancel() cancels the scope's own Job, which cancels every child and puts the scope into a terminal state. Any later launch on it creates a coroutine that's cancelled immediately and never runs. coroutineContext.cancelChildren() cancels the current children but leaves the scope's Job active, so the scope can be reused. Cancelling an individual Job stops just that subtree. I use cancel() when the owner is being destroyed for good, cancelChildren() for a reset like logout or "restart all work", and per-job cancel for replacing one operation, such as a new search query.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Call Scope Job after New launches after Use for
scope.cancel() Cancelling → Cancelled (final) Start already-cancelled. Body never runs, no error End of owner lifetime (onCleared, service onDestroy, SDK close())
scope.coroutineContext.cancelChildren() (or job.cancelChildren()) Still Active Work normally Logout, "cancel all pending", reset
job.cancel() on a single child Scope unaffected Work normally Replace one operation ("latest wins")
scope.cancel() on a scope without a Job Throws IllegalStateException: Scope cannot be cancelled because it does not have a job — Hand-rolled object : CoroutineScope without a Job

Notes:

  • cancelChildren() doesn't wait. To wait, use job.children.toList().joinAll() or cancelAndJoin on each.
  • Children cancelled this way finish with CancellationException, which doesn't propagate to the parent, so the scope stays healthy.
  • Silent failure is the dangerous part. launch on a dead scope returns a Job that's already cancelled, with no log or exception. scope.isActive (coroutineContext.isActive) tells you whether the scope is still usable.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SessionManager(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher) {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher)

    fun startPolling() { scope.launch { pollForever() } }

    // Logout: stop everything, keep the manager usable for the next login.
    fun onLogout() = scope.coroutineContext.cancelChildren()

    // App/process teardown of this component: terminal.
    fun close() = scope.cancel()
}

// BUG: manager is a singleton; cancel() on logout means polling never restarts after re-login.
fun onLogoutBroken(scope: CoroutineScope) = scope.cancel()

// Latest-wins for a single operation:
private var searchJob: Job? = null
fun search(q: String) {
    searchJob?.cancel()
    searchJob = scope.launch { results.value = repo.search(q) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling cancel() on a singleton or injected scope that outlives the component that cancels it.
  • Expecting cancelChildren() to also stop work launched into other scopes from inside these children (Q350).
