  • Calling cancel() on viewModelScope manually. The framework owns it; cancelling it breaks every later launch in that ViewModel.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do I make a cancelled scope usable again? → You can't. Create a new scope (and a new Job), or design with cancelChildren() from the start.
  2. Does cancelChildren() cancel grandchildren? → Yes, through the normal downward propagation from each child.
  3. Can cancel() take a cause? → cancel(CancellationException("logout")) or cancel("logout", cause). The cause shows in logs and invokeOnCompletion, which helps debugging.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer treats both as "cancels coroutines". The senior emphasises the terminal state, the silent no-op launches afterwards, the missing-Job exception, and matches each API to an ownership event (destroy vs reset vs replace).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a "logout → login as another user" flow, push-sync never ran again until app restart. The sync manager's singleton scope had been cancel()ed on logout, and every later launch returned an already-cancelled job without a single log line.

questions.promptHtml: When should you create your own CoroutineScope, and what rules must a class that owns a scope follow?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Framework scopes cover screens. Seniors are expected to design ownership for everything else: managers, SDKs, players, services.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I create a custom scope only when some object has a real lifecycle that framework scopes don't model, such as a media session, a socket connection, or an SDK client with close(). The rules: the scope is private, created once, with an explicit Job (usually a SupervisorJob so independent tasks don't kill each other), an injected dispatcher, and ideally a CoroutineExceptionHandler for logging. The owner cancels it exactly when its lifecycle ends. If its lifetime is part of something bigger, the Job is parented to that bigger scope so cancellation cascades. Never create a scope per call, and never expose a scope for others to cancel.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Decision ladder:

  1. Can the work be a suspend fun the caller runs in its scope? → Do that; no scope needed.
  2. Does it belong to a screen? → viewModelScope / lifecycleScope (Android scopes section).
  3. Must it outlive screens but not the app/session? → An injected app or session scope (Q351).
  4. Does a specific object have its own start/stop lifecycle? → That object owns a private scope.

Ownership checklist:

Rule Why
private val scope Nobody else can cancel() it or launch unrelated work into it
Explicit SupervisorJob() Independent tasks; one failure doesn't make the scope dead for all future work
SupervisorJob(parent = outer.job) when nested in a bigger lifetime Cancelling the outer lifetime cascades automatically
Injected dispatcher Testable with StandardTestDispatcher
CoroutineExceptionHandler that logs/reports Supervisor children without try/catch otherwise crash the process
One terminal method (close()/release()) calling scope.cancel() Clear end of life; make it idempotent
Guard public entry points after close launch on a dead scope silently does nothing. Fail loudly instead

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class PlayerController(
    parentScope: CoroutineScope,                 // e.g. session scope
    private val io: CoroutineDispatcher,
) : Closeable {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(
        SupervisorJob(parent = parentScope.coroutineContext.job) +   // cascade from parent
        io + CoroutineName("player") +
        CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> Log.e("Player", "unhandled", e) }
    )

    fun play(track: Track) {
        check(scope.isActive) { "PlayerController used after close()" }
        scope.launch { stream(track) }
    }

    override fun close() = scope.cancel()       // idempotent
}

Note: a SupervisorJob created with a parent is a child of that parent. Once close() cancels it, it detaches; if close() is never called, it stays attached until the parent is cancelled. For a short-lived child scope, that means calling close() matters.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• A new CoroutineScope(...) inside a function on every call.
  • Using a plain Job(). After the first child fails, the scope is cancelled and later work is silently dropped.
  • Forgetting close() and relying on GC. A scope with live children is reachable from its dispatcher's threads.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not just inject the app scope everywhere? → You lose the ability to cancel a subset (per-session, per-player). Group lifetimes with child scopes.
  2. Should a class implement CoroutineScope itself? → It used to be common; now it's discouraged for most classes because it exposes launch on the class's public surface. Prefer a private property.
  3. How do you test it? → Inject StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler) and assert close() cancels in-flight work (testing section).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer: "create CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO) and cancel it in onDestroy." The senior starts with "do you need a scope at all", then covers private ownership, SupervisorJob, parented Jobs for cascading lifetimes, handler, an idempotent close, and guarding against use after close.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An SDK whose client objects each held an unparented scope leaked coroutines when host apps forgot close(). Parenting each client's SupervisorJob to the SDK-level scope gave one place to shut everything down.

questions.promptHtml: What does the Job() factory return, and what are complete() and completeExceptionally() for? Why might job.join() on such a Job never return?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Developers use Job() as a lifecycle handle and then hang on join(), because unlike a coroutine's Job, a factory Job has no body that finishes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Job() and SupervisorJob() return a CompletableJob, a Job with no code of its own. A coroutine's Job completes when its body and children finish. A CompletableJob only moves toward completion when someone calls complete() (or completeExceptionally()), and then it still waits for its children. If nobody calls complete(), it stays Active forever, even with zero children, so join() on it never returns. CoroutineScope(...) creates one of these, which is why a scope's Job is ended by cancel(), not by work finishing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Coroutine Job (launch returns it) CompletableJob from Job()/SupervisorJob()
Has a body Yes No
Becomes Completing when Body returns complete() is called
Becomes final when Completing + all children done Completing + all children done
Without explicit action Completes naturally Active forever
completeExceptionally(e) n/a Fails the job with e (cancels children)

complete() returns true if the call moved the job toward completion and false if it was already completing or completed. This gives a graceful-shutdown pattern: stop accepting new work, call complete(), then join(). The join returns when in-flight children finish, unlike cancel(), which aborts them.

scopeJob = SupervisorJob()          Active (0 children) ── join() hangs forever
scopeJob.complete()                 Completing → waits children → Completed
scopeJob.cancel()                   Cancelling → children cancelled → Cancelled

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class BatchWriter(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher) {
    private val job = SupervisorJob()
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(job + dispatcher)

    @Volatile private var closing = false

    fun write(item: Item) {
        check(!closing) { "writer is closing" }    // reject new work ourselves; don't rely on Job internals
        scope.launch { db.insert(item) }
    }

    // Graceful: finish in-flight writes, then complete.
    suspend fun drainAndClose() {
        closing = true
        job.complete()
        job.join()
    }

    // BROKEN: hangs forever, nobody completes the job.
    suspend fun waitForWritesBroken() = job.join()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using scopeJob.join() to "wait until all current tasks finish". It waits forever. Use scopeJob.children.toList().joinAll() instead.
  • Calling complete() while other code keeps launching into the scope. What happens to children launched into a completing job has differed in subtle ways across releases and isn't something to rely on. Gate new work in your own code (a closing flag) before calling complete().
  • Using CompletableDeferred and CompletableJob interchangeably. CompletableDeferred<T> carries a value via complete(value); a CompletableJob carries none.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if a child of a completing Job() fails? → With a plain Job, the failure cancels the remaining children and the job ends Cancelled. With a SupervisorJob, other children continue.
  2. Does CoroutineScope(...) ever complete on its own? → No. Its Job is a CompletableJob nobody completes, so you end it with cancel().
  3. Is Job() a good one-shot signal ("wait until ready")? → Use CompletableDeferred<Unit>; its semantics (and await) are clearer.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "Job() creates a job you can cancel." The senior knows it's a CompletableJob with no body, explains why join hangs, offers complete+join as graceful drain vs cancel as abort, and joins the children snapshot to wait for in-flight work.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feature-flag "initialized" gate was modelled as a Job() that init code was supposed to complete(). One early-return path skipped the call, and every screen doing gate.join() sat on a spinner. Switching to CompletableDeferred plus a timeout made the failure visible.

questions.subtopic: coroutineContext ambiguity & the CoroutineScope receiver convention
questions.promptHtml: Inside suspend fun CoroutineScope.foo(), which coroutineContext do you get? Why is a suspend function with a CoroutineScope receiver considered a smell, and what is the right convention?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It probes whether you understand that "the scope" and "the current coroutine" can be different things, and whether you can design APIs whose lifetime semantics are clear from the signature.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: There are two coroutineContexts. One is the CoroutineScope.coroutineContext property on the receiver. The other is the top-level suspend property from kotlin.coroutines, which is the context of the coroutine actually running this code. In suspend fun CoroutineScope.foo(), the receiver's property wins resolution, so you may read the scope's Job instead of the current coroutine's. When those differ, isActive checks and launch calls bind to the wrong lifetime. currentCoroutineContext() always gives the running coroutine. The convention: suspend functions do their work and return, and use coroutineScope {} if they need concurrency. Functions that start background work and return immediately are non-suspend extensions on CoroutineScope. Never both.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
suspend fun CoroutineScope.process() {
    // Both are in scope:
    // 1) this.coroutineContext            (member of the CoroutineScope receiver), wins resolution
    // 2) kotlin.coroutines.coroutineContext (top-level suspend val)
    val ctx = coroutineContext            // → receiver's context!
}

When do they differ? Whenever the receiver isn't the scope of the current coroutine, for example appScope.process() called from inside a viewModelScope.launch. Then:

  • launch { } inside process() goes into appScope, so the work escapes the ViewModel.
  • coroutineContext.isActive reflects appScope's Job, not the caller's cancellation.
  • The function also suspends, so callers think it's "just a suspend call" that completes, while it may have left children running in another tree.

The convention as a table:

Signature Meaning Returns when
suspend fun loadAll(): Data Does work in the caller's coroutine; may use coroutineScope {} for parallelism All work done
fun CoroutineScope.startSync(): Job Starts work in the given scope Immediately
suspend fun CoroutineScope.x() Ambiguous mix Unclear. Avoid

currentCoroutineContext() was added specifically to resolve this ambiguity. Detekt's coroutines rule set has a rule for this pattern (SuspendFunWithCoroutineScopeReceiver). Check your detekt version.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// SMELL: suspend + scope receiver. Child launches go to whichever scope the caller passed.
suspend fun CoroutineScope.refreshAllBroken(ids: List<String>) {
    ids.forEach { id -> launch { repo.refresh(id) } }    // returns before work finishes; attaches to receiver
}

// Suspend style: structured, waits, cancellation follows the caller.
suspend fun refreshAll(ids: List<String>) = coroutineScope {
    ids.forEach { id -> launch { repo.refresh(id) } }
}

// Fire-and-forget style: explicit, non-suspend, returns the Job.
fun CoroutineScope.launchRefreshAll(ids: List<String>): Job = launch {
    refreshAll(ids)
}

// Reading the running coroutine's context unambiguously:
suspend fun log(msg: String) {
    val name = currentCoroutineContext()[CoroutineName]?.name
    Log.d("App", "[$name] $msg")
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using coroutineContext.isActive inside a CoroutineScope extension to check the caller's cancellation.
  • Writing flow { ... } code that reaches for an outer scope's coroutineContext captured in a lambda instead of the collector's.
  • Calling scope.launch from inside a suspend function and assuming caller cancellation reaches it (Q350).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you read the current Job in a suspend function? → currentCoroutineContext().job.
  2. Is coroutineScope { this.coroutineContext } safe? → Yes. That receiver is the new child scope of the running coroutine, so the two contexts match apart from the child Job.
  3. What about CoroutineScope as a constructor parameter? → Fine and explicit: the class says "I launch into this lifetime". Name the parameter after the lifetime (appScope, sessionScope).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average candidate has never noticed two coroutineContexts exist. The senior explains name resolution, shows how work escapes into the receiver's tree, cites currentCoroutineContext(), and enforces the suspend-vs-extension convention as an API design rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A helper suspend fun CoroutineScope.prefetch() was called with appScope from inside a screen. The screen's cancellation never reached the prefetches, and scrolling quickly through 200 items left 200 live image downloads behind.

questions.promptHtml: How do you design a custom CoroutineContext element, for example a request/trace ID that follows work across coroutines? What are the pitfalls?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows whether you can use the context as an extensibility mechanism, not just consume dispatchers, and whether you know its propagation boundaries.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I'd write an immutable class extending AbstractCoroutineContextElement with a companion object as its Key, add it at the entry point with launch(TraceId(id)) or withContext(TraceId(id)), and read it anywhere downstream with currentCoroutineContext()[TraceId]. It propagates automatically to every child, because children inherit all non-Job elements. The pitfalls: it's shared by reference, so it must be immutable. It doesn't cross into other scopes, so work launched into an app scope loses it. Code that reads ThreadLocals (MDC-style loggers, OpenTelemetry) won't see it unless the element is also a ThreadContextElement (see the ThreadLocal discussion in the suspend edge-cases section). Equality affects withContext fast paths, so a data class is a good choice.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Anatomy:

data class TraceId(val value: String) : AbstractCoroutineContextElement(TraceId) {
    companion object Key : CoroutineContext.Key<TraceId>
    override fun toString() = "TraceId($value)"
}
  • AbstractCoroutineContextElement(key) implements get/fold/minusKey for a single element.
  • The companion Key gives the element one slot: adding a new TraceId replaces the old one.
  • data class gives value equality. When the old and new contexts are equal, withContext takes a fast path and runs the block in place without re-dispatching. If they differ only in non-dispatcher elements, it runs undispatched on the same dispatcher. An identity-equality element defeats the first optimization; that's harmless but worth knowing.

Propagation boundaries:

viewModelScope.launch(TraceId("t-42")) {        ✓ has TraceId
    async { api.a() }                            ✓ inherited
    withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { db.q() }       ✓ inherited
    appScope.launch { upload() }                 ✗ appScope's context: no TraceId
    OkHttp interceptor (plain thread code)       ✗ not a coroutine; needs explicit passing or ThreadContextElement
}

Design guidance:

Concern Recommendation
Mutability Immutable value. A mutable element is shared across concurrently running children → data races
Crossing into other scopes Pass it explicitly: appScope.launch(currentCoroutineContext()[TraceId] ?: EmptyCoroutineContext) { }
Thread-based consumers Implement ThreadContextElement<S> to set/restore a ThreadLocal on each resume (cost on every dispatch)
Per-child copies CopyableThreadContextElement (since 1.6) if each child needs its own copy
Business data Avoid hiding real parameters in the context; it's invisible in signatures. Reserve it for cross-cutting concerns (tracing, auth tag for logging, test hooks)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun traced(msg: String) {
    val id = currentCoroutineContext()[TraceId]?.value ?: "-"
    Log.i("Trace", "[$id] $msg")
}

fun onPayClicked(orderId: String) = viewModelScope.launch(TraceId("pay-$orderId")) {
    traced("start")
    val quote = async { repo.quote(orderId) }                 // inherits TraceId
    withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { traced("writing receipt") }  // inherits TraceId
    traced("done ${quote.await()}")
}

// BROKEN: mutable element shared by every child; concurrent children overwrite each other.
class MutableTrace(var step: String) : AbstractCoroutineContextElement(MutableTrace) {
    companion object Key : CoroutineContext.Key<MutableTrace>
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the companion Key. The class can't be looked up idiomatically, and per-instance keys break replacement semantics.
  • Expecting the element to show up in OkHttp interceptors or plain callbacks; those run outside the coroutine.
  • Overusing context for dependency injection. It hides inputs and makes tests depend on context setup.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you get the trace ID into an OkHttp header? → Read it in the suspend layer (repository) and pass it as an explicit header/tag, or implement a ThreadContextElement and read the ThreadLocal in the interceptor, which runs on the calling thread for synchronous execute() calls.
  2. What does ThreadContextElement cost? → updateThreadContext/restoreThreadContext on every resume and suspend. Fine for one ThreadLocal, measurable if you stack many on hot paths.
  3. Can a child remove an inherited element? → withContext(EmptyCoroutineContext) doesn't remove anything. You'd override it with a sentinel value; minusKey only helps when building a new scope's context.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE engineer would typically pass the ID through every function. The senior builds a small immutable element with a Key, knows exactly where propagation stops (foreign scopes, non-coroutine threads), knows when ThreadContextElement is needed and what it costs, and warns against using context as hidden DI.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A payments team added a TraceId element and found that 30% of backend logs for a flow still lacked the ID. All of those came from work launched into an injected app scope, so they passed the element explicitly at that boundary.

questions.subtopic: Job internals (how parent and child are linked)
questions.promptHtml: Under the hood, how does a child Job attach to its parent, how does cancellation reach children, and how does a child's failure reach the parent? How does SupervisorJob change that?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Staff-level interviews check whether you can reason from the implementation when the docs run out, for example when explaining why a supervisor child "crashes the app".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Every Job is a JobSupport object whose state lives in one atomic field: a small state machine of Empty/NodeList/Finishing/final values plus a list of completion handlers. When a child coroutine starts, it calls parent.attachChild(this), which registers a child-handle node in the parent's handler list. When the parent is cancelled, it walks that list and calls parentCancelled on each child. When a child fails, it calls childCancelled(cause) on its parent handle. A regular Job returns true, cancels itself and takes responsibility for the exception. SupervisorJob overrides childCancelled to return false, so the child must handle its own exception: a CoroutineExceptionHandler, or else the uncaught handler. Completion waiting works by registering handlers on each remaining child before the parent finalizes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Simplified model. Internal names vary between versions; the shape has been stable.

JobSupport._state (atomic):
  Empty(active/new)  → no handlers yet
  NodeList           → handlers (incl. ChildHandleNodes for children, invokeOnCompletion callbacks)
  Finishing          → completing or cancelling; holds rootCause + suppressed exceptions + list
  final              → Completed value / CompletedExceptionally(cause)

Child start:
  child.initParentJob(parent) → parentHandle = parent.attachChild(child)
                                (adds ChildHandleNode to parent's list; if parent already
                                 cancelled, child is cancelled immediately)

Downward (parent → children):
  parent.cancel() → state Finishing(cancelling) → notify list → ChildHandleNode.invoke
                 → child.parentCancelled(parent) → child cancels itself

Upward (child → parent):
  child fails with e (not CancellationException)
    → child.cancelParent(e) → parentHandle.childCancelled(e)
         JobSupport:     cancelImpl(e); return true      // parent takes ownership of e
         SupervisorJob:  return false                    // parent declines
    → if false: child.handleJobException(e)             // root behaviour
         StandaloneCoroutine (launch): CoroutineExceptionHandler in context, else the uncaught handler
         DeferredCoroutine (async): no-op; exception stays in Deferred for await()

Waiting for children:
  body done → tryMakeCompleting → if children exist, register completion handler on the next child,
  resume finalization when it completes → repeat → finalize state when none left

Why this matters:

  • "Supervisor child crashes the app": because the supervisor declines, the child acts like a root and calls the uncaught exception handler.
  • Exception aggregation: the parent's Finishing state records the first exception as root cause and adds others as suppressed. That's why you see Suppressed: entries in crash logs (exception-handling section).
  • Cancellation cost is O(number of live children) handler invocations; a parent with 10,000 live children walks 10,000 nodes when it's cancelled (Q349).
  • Late attach: launching into a cancelled scope attaches to an already-cancelled parent, so the child is cancelled at once. That's the "silent no-op" from Q338.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Observable consequences of the internals:
fun main() = runBlocking {
    val sup = SupervisorJob()
    val scope = CoroutineScope(sup + CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> println("handled $e") })
    scope.launch { throw IllegalStateException("child") }.join()   // childCancelled → false → CEH
    println("supervisor active=${sup.isActive}")                     // true

    sup.cancel()
    val late = scope.launch { println("never runs") }
    println("late cancelled=${late.isCancelled}")                    // true: attached to cancelled parent
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking CoroutineExceptionHandler is "inherited and used by children". Only the coroutine that ends up handling the exception (a root, or a direct child of a supervisor) consults its own context's handler.
  • Assuming the internals use locks. They use lock-free CAS on _state, which is why cancel() is safe from any thread.
  • Building logic on Job.parent or the internal state names. They're experimental or internal.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can cancel() be called from a non-coroutine thread safely? → State transitions are atomic CAS loops; handlers run on the cancelling thread, and actual resumption is dispatched to each coroutine's dispatcher.
  2. Where does async differ in the upward path? → A child async still calls childCancelled on a regular parent, so the parent fails immediately. Only at the root or under a supervisor does it keep the exception for await().
  3. Why does invokeOnCompletion with onCancelling = true exist? → Child handles need to react when the parent starts cancelling, not when it finishes. That's the internal API the child link uses.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer stays at "parent cancels children". The senior can sketch the handler list, attachChild, the childCancelled true/false protocol, the supervisor override, and how roots handle exceptions, then use that to explain real symptoms such as crashes under supervisors, suppressed exceptions and silent no-op launches.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team argued for a week over whether supervisorScope "should" have caught a crash. Walking through childCancelled returning false showed that a crash was the designed behaviour, and the debate turned into adding per-child handling.

questions.contextHtml:
A PR in a 1.2M-MAU news app refactors the data layer. Every repository now takes a scope:

class ArticleRepository(private val api: Api, private val dao: ArticleDao) {
    fun refresh(scope: CoroutineScope) {
        scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
            val fresh = api.latest()
            dao.upsert(fresh)
        }
    }
}
// caller
fun onPullToRefresh() { repo.refresh(viewModelScope); _state.update { it.copy(refreshing = false) } }

The author's justification: "the repository shouldn't decide lifetimes; callers pass their scope". QA reports the pull-to-refresh spinner stops instantly, and errors from api.latest() show up as crashes in Crashlytics (IOException via the uncaught handler, about 0.12% of sessions on flaky networks) instead of an error banner. A reviewer suggests making the repository a CoroutineScope itself as an alternative.
questions.promptHtml: Review this design. What would you change, and when, if ever, should a data-layer API take a scope?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a try/catch inside the launch and set refreshing=false at the end." That patches symptoms but keeps an API that hides its lifetime, can't return results or errors to the caller, and can't be composed or tested as a suspend call.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Must refresh complete even if the user leaves the screen? That decides whether the caller's scope or an app scope owns it.
    • Do callers need the result or the error? The UI clearly does (banner, spinner).
    • Is dao.upsert main-safe (Room suspend)? It affects whether Dispatchers.IO is needed at all.
    • Do other callers (WorkManager, push handler) use the same API?
  2. Immediate mitigation: No incident to stop; the PR shouldn't merge as-is. If it already shipped, a hotfix that awaits the work and catches IO errors in the ViewModel stops the crash spike.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (why the symptoms happen):
    • Spinner stops instantly: refresh returns as soon as it launches, so the caller's next line runs before any network I/O. That's the fire-and-forget shape.
    • Crashes: the launch is a direct child of viewModelScope (a SupervisorJob), so its IOException is declined by the supervisor and goes to the uncaught handler.
    • Red herring: the Dispatchers.IO choice. Changing the dispatcher fixes neither.
  4. How I'd verify each: A unit test with runTest asserting refreshing stays true until the fake API returns. Inject a fake API that throws and confirm the uncaught handler fires, using CoroutineExceptionHandler capture in tests and Crashlytics stack traces showing StandaloneCoroutine frames.
  5. Root cause: The API mixes concerns. It launches into a scope it doesn't own, so the caller loses the result, the error and completion. That's exactly the "start work and return" shape, used where a suspend function was needed (Q341's convention).
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term and long-term (they're the same here): make the repository API suspend and main-safe. The caller owns the lifetime by calling it from its own coroutine.
    class ArticleRepository(private val api: Api, private val dao: ArticleDao, private val io: CoroutineDispatcher) {
    suspend fun refresh() = withContext(io) {      // main-safe; caller's cancellation applies
        dao.upsert(api.latest())
    }
}
// ViewModel
fun onPullToRefresh() = viewModelScope.launch {
    _state.update { it.copy(refreshing = true) }
    try { repo.refresh() }
    catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
    catch (e: IOException) { _state.update { it.copy(error = e.toUiError()) } }
    finally { _state.update { it.copy(refreshing = false) } }
}
    • For work that must outlive the screen (for example "mark article read" sync), the repository takes an injected, named, long-lived scope in its constructor (@ApplicationScope appScope) and documents it, keeping the public API suspend:
    suspend fun markRead(id: String) {
    appScope.launch { api.markRead(id) }.join()   // survives caller cancellation, caller still waits
}
    Even this is a deliberate exception: the caller's cancellation no longer stops the work, which must be the intent.
  7. Prevention: A review checklist item: "public data-layer functions are suspend or return Flow; a CoroutineScope parameter needs a written lifetime justification". Detekt's coroutine rules for scope-receiver smells. Tests asserting the state sequence (refreshing true → false) with Turbine.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • I wouldn't make the repository implement CoroutineScope. It exposes launch publicly, and the repository would own a lifetime it has no event to end.
    • I wouldn't put try/catch inside the repository's launch and swallow errors. The UI needs them.
    • Taking a scope per call does make sense for genuinely fire-and-forget entry points, such as an analytics track(event). There it should be a constructor-injected scope, not a per-call parameter.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "WorkManager also calls refresh. Does suspend still fit?" → Yes, better than before. CoroutineWorker.doWork() is already suspend; it calls repo.refresh() and maps exceptions to Result.retry().
  • "What if two screens refresh at once?" → Deduplication is a separate concern (a shared in-flight Deferred, or a Mutex; see the shared-state section). Scope ownership doesn't solve it.
  • "Why not return the Job from refresh(scope)?" → It still loses the error and result. You'd reinvent a worse Deferred.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite pattern I've seen: a codebase where every repository took scope: CoroutineScope. Error handling was smeared across 40 call sites, and nobody could write a test that waited for "refresh done". Converting to suspend APIs removed roughly 600 lines of callback-like plumbing and made the error banner reliable.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Keeps refresh(scope) and adds try/catch inside; doesn't explain why the spinner stops instantly.
  • Hire: Converts to a suspend API, explains the supervisor-child crash path, keeps error handling in the ViewModel with cancellation rethrown.
  • Strong hire: Also states the suspend-vs-scope-launch convention, handles the "must outlive the screen" case with a constructor-injected named scope plus join, and rejects Repository : CoroutineScope with reasons.

questions.contextHtml:
A search screen (p95 query latency 450 ms, 85k daily searches) shows stale results: typing "kotl" then quickly "kotlin flow" sometimes leaves the "kotl" results on screen. Also, LeakCanary in internal builds occasionally reports SearchViewModel retained after leaving the screen (about 1 in 40 sessions in QA runs).

class SearchUseCase(private val api: SearchApi) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(q: String): List<Hit> {
        val scope = CoroutineScope(currentCoroutineContext() + SupervisorJob())
        return scope.async(Dispatchers.IO) { api.search(q) }.await()
    }
}

class SearchViewModel(private val search: SearchUseCase) : ViewModel() {
    private var job: Job? = null
    val results = MutableStateFlow<List<Hit>>(emptyList())

    fun onQuery(q: String) {
        job?.cancel()
        job = viewModelScope.launch {
            val hits = search(q)
            results.value = hits
        }
    }
}

A teammate suspects MutableStateFlow conflation and wants to switch to SharedFlow.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug(s), explain the stale results and the leak mechanically, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use flatMapLatest or debounce." That might hide the symptom, but the use case is still detached from cancellation, and the candidate can't explain why job?.cancel() doesn't work.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is api.search a Retrofit suspend call (cancellable)? Do stale results appear only when the first query is slower than the second? Is the leak trace pointing at a coroutine or a lambda capture?
  2. Immediate mitigation: No hotfix needed; it's a QA finding. If it were live, a guard if (q == latestQuery) before writing results would stop the visible symptom while the real fix lands.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (Top) CoroutineScope(currentCoroutineContext() + SupervisorJob()) replaces the caller's Job with a fresh SupervisorJob, so the async isn't a child of the ViewModel's launch.
    • StateFlow conflation is a red herring: conflation drops intermediate values, it doesn't resurrect old ones.
    • A missing debounce makes the race more frequent but isn't the cause.
  4. How I'd verify each: A runTest unit test with a fake API where query 1 completes after query 2: assert results equal query 2's. Log currentCoroutineContext().job inside the async, or enable debug mode and dump coroutines with DebugProbes after job.cancel(); the async will still be listed as active.
  5. Root cause:
    • When onQuery("kotlin flow") cancels the old job, cancellation reaches the outer launch, which is suspended in await(). await is cancellable, so the outer coroutine resumes with CancellationException... except the race. If the detached async completes and resumes the waiter before the cancellation is processed, results.value = hits can still run for the stale query, because the network call itself was never cancelled and kept racing.
    • More concretely: the detached async keeps running to completion for every query (wasting requests), and its continuation holds the outer coroutine's frame. That frame references the ViewModel through results and search. For a slow request, the ViewModel is retained after onCleared() until the network call returns or times out (OkHttp default read timeout 10 s, longer with retries), which is what LeakCanary sees.
    • Each call also creates a new unowned scope that is never cancelled.
  6. Fix: 
    class SearchUseCase(private val api: SearchApi, private val io: CoroutineDispatcher) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(q: String): List<Hit> = withContext(io) { api.search(q) }
}
    With withContext, the request is a child of the launching coroutine. job?.cancel() cancels the HTTP call (Retrofit suspend calls cancel the OkHttp Call), and no stale result can be written after cancellation, since withContext checks cancellation on return. Long-term, model search as queryFlow.debounce(300).mapLatest { search(it) } (operators section) so "latest wins" is declarative.
  7. Prevention: A lint/detekt rule flagging CoroutineScope( inside function bodies and Job()/SupervisorJob() arguments to builders. A unit test for out-of-order completion. A code review rule: use cases are plain suspend functions.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't switch to SharedFlow; it changes event semantics and fixes nothing. I wouldn't add a NonCancellable or a GlobalScope "to be safe". If the request must not be cancelled (rare for search), that's a product decision and needs an explicitly owned scope.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why did the author write that line?" → Probably to stop a search error from cancelling the ViewModel's other work. viewModelScope is already a supervisor; a try/catch in onQuery is the right tool.
  • "Is currentCoroutineContext() + SupervisorJob() ever right?" → Only with an explicit parent: SupervisorJob(currentCoroutineContext().job). Even then, supervisorScope {} says the same thing more clearly.
  • "Would coroutineScope { async { } }.await() work?" → Yes, but async immediately followed by await is just withContext.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: In a composite case, an e-commerce search sent about 2.3x more backend queries than keystroke analytics predicted. Every superseded query still ran to completion through a detached scope. Removing one line cut search QPS by more than half.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames StateFlow, or adds debounce without spotting the detached scope.
  • Hire: Identifies that + SupervisorJob() replaces the Job, explains that cancellation doesn't reach the request, and fixes it with withContext.
  • Strong hire: Also explains the leak via retained continuation frames, quantifies the wasted requests, proposes mapLatest for the long term, and adds lint plus an out-of-order test.

questions.subtopic: Job vs SupervisorJob in an owned scope
questions.contextHtml:
An analytics uploader in a fitness app (400k DAU) batches events every 30 s:

@Singleton
class EventUploader @Inject constructor(private val api: EventsApi, private val store: EventStore) {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO)

    fun schedule() {
        scope.launch {
            while (isActive) {
                val batch = store.next(500)
                if (batch.isNotEmpty()) { api.send(batch); store.ack(batch) }
                delay(30_000)
            }
        }
    }
    fun flushNow() { scope.launch { api.send(store.all()) } }
}

After a release, the data team sees event volume drop 18% day over day. The drop is concentrated on users on flaky networks (rural, subway). Crashlytics shows nothing. On-device event backlog (store.size) for affected users grows to 50k+. A teammate suspects a server-side rate limit (a few 429s show in backend logs).
questions.promptHtml: What happened, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add retry with backoff for the 429s." The rate limit is real but minor. Retries don't explain why uploading stops entirely and permanently for the session.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did this release add flushNow() (yes, a new "flush on workout end")? Does uploading resume after an app restart? Is there a CoroutineExceptionHandler anywhere? Did anything change in api.send error behaviour?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Events persist in store, so no data is lost yet. Ship a hotfix (or flip a remote-config flag that disables flushNow) and rely on the backlog draining after the fix. Raise the backlog cap so old events aren't evicted.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (Top) CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO) silently adds a plain Job(). The first uncaught IOException from either coroutine fails its child, which cancels the scope's Job. That stops the polling loop, and every later launch is a silent no-op until process death.
    • The 429 rate limit adds failures but isn't the mechanism.
    • Doze/background restrictions: they would delay uploads, not stop them until restart.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add a debug log of scope.isActive and of invokeOnCompletion { cause -> } on the scope Job; in a test, make the fake API throw once and assert the loop stops. Crashlytics is empty because the exception was propagated to the scope's Job, not to the uncaught handler. A plain-Job parent takes ownership of child failures, and the root scope object has no coroutine to report it. Verify with a unit test using runTest, StandardTestDispatcher and a throwing fake.
  5. Root cause: Failure-up semantics with a regular Job (Q335): one child failure cancels the parent scope, and a cancelled scope is terminal (Q338). The new flushNow() call made a failing child far more likely on bad networks, because it was a one-shot launch with no try/catch.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term:
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(
    SupervisorJob() + io + CoroutineName("event-uploader") +
    CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> logger.report(e) }      // nothing escapes silently
)
    • Long-term: handle errors inside the loop, so one bad batch doesn't end it, and move periodic upload to WorkManager with constraints and backoff.
    scope.launch {
    while (isActive) {
        try { uploadOnce() }
        catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
        catch (e: IOException) { backoff.next().let { delay(it) }; continue }
        delay(30_000)
    }
}
  7. Prevention: A metric for "uploader alive" (timestamp of last successful send) with an alert on fleet-wide staleness. A unit test asserting the scope survives one failing child. A review rule: every custom scope declares an explicit SupervisorJob() and a handler.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't wrap everything in runCatching; it swallows CancellationException and would keep the loop "alive" through cancellation. I wouldn't recreate the scope on failure. Hiding a dead scope behind a new one masks bugs; SupervisorJob plus a handler is the documented pattern.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "With SupervisorJob but no handler, what happens on failure?" → The child's exception goes to the uncaught handler and the app crashes. That's louder than before, but now a crash. The handler is not optional.
  • "Why didn't while (isActive) keep the loop alive?" → isActive became false because the scope was cancelled. The loop exited correctly; it's the parent that died.
  • "Could 429 handling still matter?" → Yes, as a separate improvement: honour Retry-After with backoff.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: In a composite incident, a crash-free dashboard hid an outage: the logging pipeline itself had a dead plain-Job scope, so the very system meant to report failures had stopped silently. "Liveness" metrics for background loops became a standard requirement.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Focuses on 429 retries; doesn't know CoroutineScope() adds a Job or why the scope dies.
  • Hire: Explains that child failure cancels the plain-Job scope permanently and switches to SupervisorJob with error handling in the loop.
  • Strong hire: Also explains why Crashlytics was silent, adds the handler, liveness metrics and a regression test, and avoids runCatching swallowing cancellation.

questions.subtopic: Failure policy per operation (coroutineScope vs supervisorScope)
questions.contextHtml:
A photo-backup feature uploads selected photos in parallel (batch of up to 50, 4 concurrent via a Semaphore). After a release that added server-side size validation, support tickets rise: "I backed up 50 photos and only 3 uploaded". Logs per batch:

12:01:03.120 upload start x50
12:01:04.870 HTTP 413 Payload Too Large  photo=IMG_2231.HEIC (48 MB)
12:01:04.874 kotlinx.coroutines.JobCancellationException: Parent job is Cancelling  (x46)
12:01:04.880 BackupViewModel: backup failed: HttpException 413

The code:

suspend fun backup(photos: List<Photo>) = coroutineScope {
    photos.map { p -> async { limiter.withPermit { api.upload(p) } } }.awaitAll()
}

OkHttp timeouts were also raised from 10 s to 60 s in the same release, and a teammate suspects they're involved.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the logs, decide the correct failure policy, and implement it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch to supervisorScope and it's fixed." Half right: awaitAll() still throws the first failure, so the batch still "fails" in the UI. The candidate also never asks what the product wants on partial failure.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should one bad photo abort the batch, or should we upload everything possible and report the failures? (Product: report per photo.) Are uploads idempotent if retried? Is there a resumable-upload API for large files?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side, temporarily raise the size limit or return a client-skippable error. Client-side, a hotfix with per-photo handling.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (Top) coroutineScope all-or-nothing semantics. The 413 failure cancels the parent scope, which cancels the 46 queued/in-flight siblings. That's the JobCancellationException: Parent job is Cancelling lines.
    • The timeouts are a red herring: the failure happens within 1.7 s.
    • The Semaphore is not the cause; cancelled waiters simply leave the permit queue.
  4. How I'd verify each: A unit test with a fake API failing photo #2 of 10: assert the other 9 were cancelled under coroutineScope and complete under the new policy. In the logs, the 46 cancellation lines all arrive within 4 ms of the 413, which confirms the cascade.
  5. Root cause: Failure-up semantics. In a regular scope, the first failing async child cancels the parent and all siblings, and awaitAll rethrows. Right policy for a transaction, wrong one for independent uploads.
  6. Fix: 
    sealed interface UploadResult { data class Ok(val id: String) : UploadResult; data class Failed(val photo: Photo, val error: Throwable) : UploadResult }

suspend fun backup(photos: List<Photo>): List<UploadResult> = supervisorScope {
    photos.map { p ->
        async {
            try { UploadResult.Ok(limiter.withPermit { api.upload(p) }) }
            catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }            // real cancellation still propagates
            catch (e: Exception) { UploadResult.Failed(p, e) }
        }
    }.awaitAll()
}
    Catching per child already stops propagation, so coroutineScope would also work here. I use supervisorScope as defence in depth, and because it states the intent: independent children. Long-term, validate size client-side before upload and add resumable uploads for big files.
  7. Prevention: A design-review question for every parallel decomposition: "is this all-or-nothing or best-effort?", written in the KDoc. Tests for both behaviours. A metric for per-batch success ratio so a cascade shows up as a cliff.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't use supervisorScope with bare awaitAll() and no per-child handling; the first failure is still rethrown. I wouldn't swallow CancellationException in the per-child catch. If the batch were transactional (for example multi-part atomic order), I'd keep coroutineScope deliberately.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "What if the user cancels the backup mid-way?" → Cancelling the outer coroutine still cancels everything under the supervisor; supervision is only about child failures.
  • "Why not launch instead of async?" → You'd lose the per-photo results, and under a supervisor each failing launch needs a handler or it crashes.
  • "Memory with 5,000 photos?" → 5,000 Deferreds is fine (a few hundred bytes each), but chunk the list so results stream progressively and memory stays bounded.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: In a composite case, a document-scanning app's "export all" silently became all-or-nothing after a refactor from callbacks to coroutineScope. The behaviour change was never written down. The fix included a one-line KDoc, "best-effort: failures are reported per item", which prevented the next regression.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames the timeouts; can't explain the JobCancellationException lines.
  • Hire: Explains the sibling cascade, uses per-child handling with supervisorScope, and rethrows cancellation.
  • Strong hire: Asks for the product policy first, explains why supervisorScope alone isn't enough with awaitAll, keeps all-or-nothing where it fits, and adds metrics and tests for both behaviours.

questions.contextHtml: A ride-hailing app (2M MAU, Android 8-14, 35% low-RAM devices) has 140 call sites of GlobalScope.launch, added over six years. Crashlytics shows OutOfMemoryError at 0.4% of sessions, and heap dumps show many StandaloneCoroutine objects holding Activity references via lambdas. The team wants to remove GlobalScope in one 3-week push, without changing user-visible behaviour. Rough categories from a grep: about 90 are "do this for the screen" (load, submit), about 30 are "must finish even if the user leaves" (send receipt, upload trip rating), about 20 are periodic or app-lifetime loops (location ping, token refresh timer). A manager proposes a regex replace of GlobalScope with a single shared appScope everywhere.
questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replace with viewModelScope / lifecycleScope." That is right for one category only. A blind find-and-replace changes behaviour for the 30 must-finish calls (they would now be cancelled on screen exit), and the manager's single appScope just renames GlobalScope.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which calls have user-visible side effects that must complete? Are any calls touching views? Do we have crash/ANR dashboards and staged rollout (so each batch can be measured)? Is Hilt in place for injecting scopes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: The OOM is a leak: lambdas passed to GlobalScope capture Activities. First, stop the bleeding in the worst offenders (top 5 by heap-dump retained size) by moving them into lifecycleScope, ahead of the larger migration.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (Top) screen-bound work in GlobalScope capturing views/Activities. Then: long-running loops never cancelled. Red herring: the dispatcher choice.
  4. How I'd verify each: LeakCanary in debug builds plus heap dump analysis for GC roots (the path is dispatcher thread -> continuation -> lambda -> Activity). Count live coroutines with the debug probes during QA sessions. Compare OOM rate per release in Crashlytics.
  5. Root cause: GlobalScope has no Job, so nothing ties the coroutine's lifetime to the screen. Any captured reference lives until the coroutine ends, and a stuck or slow request can pin an Activity for the full timeout.
  6. Fix: classify, then migrate by category, not by regex.
    • Screen-bound (90): viewModelScope for logic, lifecycleScope/repeatOnLifecycle only for UI work. Where the code was calling suspend APIs, often the right move is making the enclosing function suspend and deleting the launch.
    • Must-finish (30): not a screen scope. Move them to a named, injected, application-lifetime scope with a SupervisorJob and a handler, or better, to WorkManager when it must survive process death (receipts and ratings should be persisted and retried, not kept in memory).
    @Qualifier annotation class ApplicationScope
@Provides @Singleton @ApplicationScope
fun appScope(@DefaultDispatcher d: CoroutineDispatcher): CoroutineScope =
    CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + d + CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> crashReporter.log(e) })
    • Loops (20): owned by the component that starts and stops them (location manager, session manager), each with its own cancellable Job or child scope, not by whichever screen happened to call them. Roll out in 4 batches behind staged rollout (1%, 10%, 50%, 100%), watching OOM, crash and "completion" metrics (receipts sent / trips completed) so a regression in the must-finish category is visible.
  7. Prevention: Detekt GlobalCoroutineUsage rule (it exists in the detekt coroutines rule set; check version) set to error, with a baseline for the remaining sites. Review checklist: "who owns this lifetime?" Lint for lifecycleScope.launch capturing ViewModel-owned logic.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't regex-replace to a global appScope: it removes none of the leaks and hides the intent. I wouldn't move must-finish calls to viewModelScope; that silently drops receipts when users leave quickly. I'd accept that some of the 30 need a product answer ("is a lost rating OK?").

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "The app scope has a SupervisorJob and a handler. Is it now safe to launch anything there?" -> No. It holds captured references for the work's duration, so lambdas must not capture Activities or Views, and work should be bounded by timeouts.
  • "How do you prove you didn't drop receipts?" -> Server-side receipt counts per trip before and after each rollout stage, plus an on-device counter.
  • "Why WorkManager for some?" -> App scope doesn't survive process death; WorkManager persists the request and applies constraints and backoff.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: In a composite case, a team did the mechanical replacement with viewModelScope. Two weeks later, finance noticed a 1.5% drop in receipts emailed. Users backed out of the screen right after payment, cancelling the send. The audit became "classify by required lifetime" and the migration was redone.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Global replace to viewModelScope or a single appScope; no mention of behaviour change.
  • Hire: Classifies by lifetime, uses screen scopes for screen work and an injected app scope or WorkManager for must-finish work.
  • Strong hire: Adds staged rollout with completion metrics, lint enforcement, a leak-first mitigation order, and explicit awareness that app scope still holds captured references.

questions.contextHtml: A messaging app indexes attachments for offline search. An IndexingManager has one private scope (SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) and does scope.launch { index(file) } for every incoming file. With 5k files per user this worked. A new bulk-import feature produces up to 400k files per import. Observed on mid-range devices (4 GB RAM): heap grows by roughly 90 MB during import, GC pauses of 40-60 ms show up as jank, and tapping "Cancel import" (scope.cancel()) freezes the UI for about 700 ms. Log excerpt: Choreographer: Skipped 42 frames!. Someone suggests simply moving to Dispatchers.IO for more threads.
questions.promptHtml: What is going on, and how do you design this to scale?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use IO instead of Default, or add a delay between launches." That adds threads and doesn't address launching 400k coroutines up front, so memory and the cancel storm stay.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is indexing CPU-bound (parsing, tokenizing) or I/O-bound? How many can usefully run at once? Does import need to be resumable? Is the work list already in a DB?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap the work in flight. A quick hotfix is a Semaphore or a fixed pool of worker coroutines, which immediately bounds live coroutines.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (Top) Launching one coroutine per file creates up to 400k live coroutines, each with a Job, continuation, captured lambda and a node in the scope's children list. Order of magnitude is hundreds of bytes each, so 400k times about 200 B is roughly 80-100 MB, which is consistent with the heap growth. I'd confirm per-object sizes with a heap dump rather than trust the estimate.
    • The 700 ms freeze: scope.cancel() walks every child and notifies each, 400k handler invocations, then each resumes with CancellationException. Doing this on the main thread (the cancel button's thread) blocks it.
    • More threads (IO): red herring. The work is queued, not thread-starved.
  4. How I'd verify each: Android Studio memory profiler allocation tracking (count of StandaloneCoroutine and LockFreeLinkedList nodes), Perfetto slices for the main thread during cancel(), DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() count in a debug build. A microbenchmark of launching and cancelling N coroutines to get cost per coroutine on the target device.
  5. Root cause: "Unbounded fan-out". Coroutines are cheap, not free; the cost scales with live coroutines, and the scope's child bookkeeping makes cancel() O(live children), run synchronously on the caller's thread.
  6. Fix: Bound the concurrency and bound the live set. A fixed worker pool pulling from a Channel (or paging from the DB): 
    fun startImport(files: Flow<File>) = scope.launch {
    val work = Channel<File>(capacity = 64)          // bounded: producer suspends when full
    launch { files.collect { work.send(it) }; work.close() }
    repeat(4) {                                      // 4 workers ~ cores
        launch { for (f in work) index(f) }
    }
}
    Live coroutines are about 6, cancellation is O(6), and memory is flat. Alternatively flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) over a Flow of files (operators and channels sections cover the details). Keep the work list in the DB so import is resumable after cancel or process death. Keep the import under its own child Job so "Cancel import" cancels importJob, not the whole manager scope.
  7. Prevention: A rule of thumb in review: "launch in a loop over unbounded input needs a bound". A benchmark test that imports 100k synthetic files and asserts a max live coroutine count and heap delta. Alert on janky frames during import in the field.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't launch lazily with CoroutineStart.LAZY for 400k jobs; that still allocates them all. I wouldn't call cancel() from main on a huge tree; even after the fix I'd cancel from a background dispatcher if the child count could still be large. Worker count is a tuning knob: more workers help only if the work is I/O-bound.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Would async and awaitAll on 400k items be better?" -> No: it holds 400k Deferreds and their results in memory at once.
  • "How do you tune the worker count?" -> CPU-bound: about the core count (Default dispatcher already limits to that). I/O-bound: higher, bounded by what the disk or network handles; measure throughput versus workers.
  • "Why did Default not starve the UI?" -> It didn't; the jank came from GC pressure and the main-thread cancel, not CPU contention.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite case: a photo-sync feature "worked in QA with 200 photos" and OOMed on a tester's library of 60k. The postmortem line was "coroutines are cheap, unbounded coroutines are not".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests changing dispatcher or adding delays.
  • Hire: Identifies unbounded fan-out as the memory and cancel cost, and bounds it with a worker pool or semaphore.
  • Strong hire: Quantifies the per-coroutine cost with a measure-it caveat, explains O(children) cancellation on the main thread, separates the import Job from the manager scope, and makes the work list resumable.

questions.contextHtml:
A banking app's logout flow calls sessionScope.coroutineContext.cancelChildren() and clears the token store. After a release, security QA finds that after logout, a "transactions" screen's prefetch still fires authenticated requests for up to 20 s, and 0.3% of logouts end with a crash: NullPointerException: token from an OkHttp interceptor reading the cleared store. The prefetch code:

class TxRepository(private val api: TxApi, private val appScope: CoroutineScope) {
    suspend fun prefetchAccounts(ids: List<String>) {
        ids.forEach { id -> appScope.launch { cache.put(id, api.transactions(id)) } }
    }
}

It's called from sessionScope.launch { repo.prefetchAccounts(ids) }. sessionScope is a child scope of appScope created per login. Backend sees about 11 authenticated calls per logout after the token is revoked, returning 401.
questions.promptHtml: Explain why cancelChildren() did not stop the work, and fix it, including the logout design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Call appScope.cancel() on logout too." That kills the app-wide scope for every later feature. Or "null-check the token in the interceptor", which hides a lifetime bug.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which scope should own prefetch: the session or the app? Does anything legitimately need to survive logout (for example a "log out" API call itself)? How many other places launch into appScope from session-bound code?
  2. Immediate mitigation: The 401 calls are annoying; the crash is user-visible. Ship a guard in the interceptor that fails fast with an IOException("no session") instead of NPE (a typed error the callers already handle), and server-side nothing is needed since the token is revoked.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (Top) prefetchAccounts launches into appScope, a different tree from sessionScope. cancelChildren() on the session's Job only reaches coroutines in its tree (Q341: launching into a scope you hold, not the caller's).
    • The caller's launch finishes immediately after it spawns the children, so the sessionScope tree has no live children for the loop to cancel. It looks like a no-op.
    • Red herring: cancelChildren vs cancel. Both only reach children in the same tree.
  4. How I'd verify each: Debug-build coroutine dump after logout (the live coroutines show appScope as their parent chain). A unit test: call prefetchAccounts under a test sessionScope, cancel the session's children, and assert the in-flight API fake is cancelled. Check coroutineContext.job.children of both scopes.
  5. Root cause: A suspend function that launches into an injected foreign scope detaches its work from the caller's cancellation. The structure is sessionScope -> launch(caller) and appScope -> N prefetch coroutines, with no edge between them.
  6. Fix: Make the function a plain suspend function, so the work stays in the caller's tree: 
    suspend fun prefetchAccounts(ids: List<String>) = coroutineScope {
    ids.forEach { id -> launch { cache.put(id, api.transactions(id)) } }   // children of the caller
}
    Now sessionScope.coroutineContext.cancelChildren() cancels the caller, which cancels the prefetch children, and the OkHttp calls are cancelled (Retrofit suspend). Logout design: (1) cancel and join the session tree first (sessionJob.cancelAndJoin() on a background dispatcher), (2) only then clear tokens, so no in-flight work can observe a half-cleared session. (3) Parent the session scope to the app scope's Job so app shutdown still cascades.
  7. Prevention: A review rule against injecting a broader-lived scope into a function that serves a narrower-lived caller. A logout integration test asserting zero network calls after the logout completes (MockWebServer request count). The interceptor uses a typed "session closed" error.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't appScope.cancel(). I wouldn't make logout wait without a timeout: withTimeout(2_000) around the join, then force-clear, because a stuck non-cooperative child shouldn't block logout. For the one thing that must outlive logout (the revoke-token API call), I'd run it explicitly in the app scope.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why join before clearing tokens?" -> cancel only requests cancellation; coroutines in Cancelling still run finally blocks and in-flight interceptors. Joining makes the ordering explicit.
  • "What if some third-party SDK launches into its own scope?" -> Then you need that SDK's close() or logout(); document it in the logout sequence.
  • "Is cancelChildren() right for logout with a singleton?" -> Yes (Q338), as long as the scope is the session's and re-created or reusable for the next login.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a "clear data" button zeroed the user store while prefetches kept running in a repository-owned scope. The next user logging in on the same device briefly saw the previous user's cached rows when the stale coroutines wrote late. The fix was lifetimes plus a session ID check on cache writes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Null-checks the token or cancels the app scope.
  • Hire: Explains that launching into appScope leaves the session tree, converts to a suspend function with coroutineScope, and fixes the logout order.
  • Strong hire: Adds cancelAndJoin with a timeout, a session-ID guard on late writes, an integration test on request counts, and identifies the cases that must stay in app scope.

questions.contextHtml: You're designing the lifetimes layer for a fintech app with 300 screens-equivalents, Hilt, and a multi-account feature (user can switch accounts without restarting the app). Requirements: (a) work started by a screen should stop when the screen goes away, unless it is explicitly "must finish"; (b) must-finish work (submit payment confirmation, upload KYC photo) should survive screen exit; (c) everything account-specific must stop on account switch or logout; (d) one failed background task must not take down the others; (e) all of it must be testable. A colleague proposes one @Singleton CoroutineScope injected everywhere.
questions.promptHtml: Design the scope hierarchy and rules.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "One app scope with SupervisorJob." That can't express requirement (c): account-specific work would need manual tracking, and "cancel the app scope on switch" kills app-wide work.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must "must-finish" work survive process death (then WorkManager, not a scope)? How long can it take? Are there app-wide jobs not tied to any account (remote config refresh, analytics)? Do multiple accounts run concurrently or one active at a time?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident. Ship the hierarchy before the multi-account feature, not after.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (design options): flat singleton scope (fails c); a scope per account chained under an app scope (fits all); WorkManager only (fails a: too heavy for UI-bound work, and no in-memory results).
  4. How I'd verify each: A test per requirement: cancel screen -> screen work stops, must-finish continues; switch account -> account scope's children stop and app-level ones continue; fail one child -> siblings alive; all with StandardTestDispatcher injected.
  5. Root cause / design reasoning: Cancellation boundaries should mirror ownership boundaries. Each boundary is a Job in a tree.
  6. Design: 
    AppScope      (SupervisorJob, Default, handler)         lives for the process
 ├── AccountScope[acct-1]  (SupervisorJob parented to AppScope)   cancelled on switch/logout
 │     ├── must-finish work for that account (payment confirm, KYC upload)
 │     └── account-bound loops (sync, polling)
 └── app-wide work (config refresh, analytics)
Screen scopes: viewModelScope / lifecycleScope (framework-owned)
    @Singleton
class AccountScopes @Inject constructor(@ApplicationScope private val app: CoroutineScope,
                                        @DefaultDispatcher private val d: CoroutineDispatcher) {
    @Volatile private var current: CoroutineScope? = null
    @Synchronized fun open(id: String): CoroutineScope {
        current?.cancel()                                       // old account's work stops
        return CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob(app.coroutineContext.job) + d +
                CoroutineName("account-$id") + app.coroutineContext[CoroutineExceptionHandler]!!)
            .also { current = it }
    }
    @Synchronized fun close() { current?.cancel(); current = null }
}
    Rules: (1) screen code never launches into AccountScope/AppScope directly; it calls an injected use case whose suspend function delegates "must finish" work to the right scope and joins so the screen can show a result but the work isn't cancelled if the screen leaves. (2) Every scope has SupervisorJob + handler + injected dispatcher. (3) A scope is created and cancelled by exactly one owner. (4) Must-finish work that must survive process death goes to WorkManager; scopes are for in-process lifetime only. (5) Per-task timeouts; scopes don't make work finite. 
    suspend fun confirmPayment(p: Payment) =
    accountScope.async { api.confirm(p) }.await()   // screen leaving cancels the await, not the confirm
  7. Prevention: An architecture test (ArchUnit/Konsist style) banning CoroutineScope( construction outside the lifetimes module. Lint for GlobalScope. Documentation of the scope table (who owns, when cancelled). Tests per requirement.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: More scopes means more places to get lifetimes wrong; I'd keep exactly three kinds. I wouldn't give the screen layer a raw handle to the account scope. I wouldn't treat "in-memory scope" as durable: a killed process loses the confirm unless it's persisted first (outbox pattern with WorkManager).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "User taps pay, leaves the screen, account scope still running, then user switches accounts. What happens to the payment confirm?" -> It's cancelled with the old account scope. If that is unacceptable, the confirm must be persisted (outbox) and executed by WorkManager independent of switching.
  • "Why parent AccountScope's Job to AppScope's?" -> So process-level shutdown, tests' scope teardown, or an app-wide kill switch cascades.
  • "Singleton scope in tests?" -> Provide a test module that supplies TestScope-backed scopes with StandardTestDispatcher and cancels them in teardown.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite case: a team with one global scope implemented account switching by tracking Job handles in a map. Every new feature forgot to register. Moving to a scope-per-account tree deleted the registry, and "stale data from previous account" bugs disappeared.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: One singleton scope; no way to cancel per account.
  • Hire: Tree of AppScope -> AccountScope with SupervisorJobs, screen scopes separate, injected dispatchers.
  • Strong hire: Also covers the screen-to-must-finish delegation pattern with async + await, WorkManager/outbox for process death, parenting Jobs, an architecture test, and tests per requirement.

questions.subtopic: Post-incident review of a scope leak
questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review. Three weeks after a release, a video-chat app (800k DAU) saw: median memory at 6 minutes of use up 38%, "Out of memory" crash rate up from 0.15% to 0.9%, and battery complaints (background CPU wake-ups). A bisect landed on a "resilience" PR whose description said: "wrap network work so one failing call can't kill the screen". Merged code:

abstract class BaseViewModel : ViewModel() {
    protected fun safeLaunch(block: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit): Job =
        viewModelScope.launch(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO + handler) { block() }

    protected suspend fun <T> safeIo(block: suspend () -> T): T =
        withContext(Job() + Dispatchers.IO) { block() }

    private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> Log.e("VM", "failed", e) }
}

It is used by ~120 ViewModels. Memory leak traces show ChatViewModel retained with SupervisorJob nodes and a while(true) { delay(5000); refreshPresence() } loop still running after the chat screen was closed.
questions.promptHtml: Run the review: causes, contributing factors, fixes, and what process changes you'd make.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "A developer made a mistake; we'll be more careful." No mechanism, no systemic fix, and no mention of why tests and review missed it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What did the PR claim to fix (which crash)? Are there ViewModels that depend on the new swallowing behaviour? Did tests exercise screen exit?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the BaseViewModel change (single-file revert covering 120 ViewModels) behind a staged rollout; hotfix the presence loop ownership first if revert is blocked. Watch OOM rate, memory at 6 minutes and wake-ups per hour.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (Top) launch(SupervisorJob() + ...) replaces the scope's Job (Q337), so every safeLaunch coroutine is outside viewModelScope, never cancelled in onCleared(). Loops like refreshPresence run forever, each retaining the ViewModel (and its repositories, caches, bitmaps).
    • withContext(Job() + ...): the same detachment inside suspend functions. Caller cancellation no longer stops the IO block, so rapid screen changes pile up in-flight requests.
    • The handler (swallowing exceptions) is a contributing factor: errors in leaked loops produce a log line instead of a crash, so the leak was never loud.
    • Red herring: Dispatchers.IO choice.
  4. How I'd verify each: LeakCanary: path Thread -> continuation -> ChatViewModel. A test: call safeLaunch { while(true) delay(1) }, call onCleared via ViewModelStore.clear(), assert the Job is still active. Coroutine dump after screen exit. Perfetto/battery tools to count wake-ups from the 5 s loops.
  5. Root cause: The author wanted "failure isolation" but viewModelScope is already a supervisor, and the way to add error handling is a try/catch or a handler, not a Job argument. Passing a Job severs both cancellation directions (Q337), so lifetimes of 120 ViewModels' background work silently became "forever".
  6. Fix: 
    abstract class BaseViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> Log.e("VM", "failed", e); report(e) }

    protected fun safeLaunch(block: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit): Job =
        viewModelScope.launch(handler) { block() }      // keeps the parent link; handler logs root failures

    protected suspend fun <T> safeIo(block: suspend () -> T): T =
        withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { block() }         // child of the caller; cancellation flows
}
    Per-call error mapping (UI states) stays in try/catch inside the lambda with CancellationException rethrown. Presence loop moves to a repeatOnLifecycle-driven flow or an explicit start/stop owned by the screen.
  7. Prevention: (a) Lint/detekt: no Job/SupervisorJob arguments to launch/async/withContext; Sonar S6306 covers part of this. (b) A base-class test suite: every wrapper must pass "cancelled when onCleared" and "caller cancellation reaches the block". (c) A memory regression guard in CI (heap after N navigations, LeakCanary in instrumented tests). (d) Review process: base-class changes touching lifetimes require two reviewers and a staged rollout; the PR description must state the lifetime impact. (e) Alert on OOM rate by release at 1% rollout.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't keep safeLaunch swallowing everything: log-and-report is fine, but a handler that hides programmer errors turns crashes into silent corruption; I'd decide per error class. I wouldn't blame the author. The system allowed a one-line change in a 120-consumer base class with no lifetime test. I'd avoid a blanket "ban base classes" reaction.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "How do you know the blast radius?" -> Count call sites of the two wrappers; retained-size ranking from heap dumps by ViewModel class; cohort the OOM rate by screens visited.
  • "Should safeLaunch exist at all?" -> A thin wrapper adding the handler is fine; anything richer (retry, loading state) belongs in explicit operators or use cases.
  • "Why was the crash rate up but 'crash-free' dashboards didn't flag leaks?" -> Leaks surface as OOM later in the session; track OOM, memory at fixed session times and background CPU, not only crashes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite review: the "fix" PR was written to silence one noisy crash with 0.02% frequency and created a 6x larger one. The lasting change was adding a lifetime test to the base class, which takes 20 lines and has caught two later regressions.
